# BasicMed (US) Aircraft Operating Limits — Current Federal Rule

## Governing authority and currency
Source of record: 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), as amended by the FAA final rule implementing section 828 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (published 2024-11-18, FR doc 2024-26935), confirmed verbatim in the current eCFR text of 61.113(i)(1) and in the CFR-2025 annual edition (14 CFR vol. 2, sec. 61.113). The operative statutory basis is FESSA sec. 2307(j) as amended, codified at 49 U.S.C. 44703 note. As-of date of this answer: current text as fetched 2026-11-17.

## Operative regulatory text (verbatim, 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1))

> "(i) A private pilot may act as pilot in command or serve as a required flightcrew member of an aircraft without holding a medical certificate issued under part 67 of this chapter provided the pilot holds a valid U.S. driver's license, meets the requirements of § 61.23(c)(3), and complies with this section and all of the following conditions and limitations:
> (1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter; ..."

The FAA BasicMed page states the same limits in plain language: aircraft "authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants", "maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds"; operation "Carries not more than six passengers".

## The three limits

| # | Limit | Value | Unit | Source wording |
|---|-------|-------|------|----------------|
| 1 | Maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of the aircraft | 12,500 | lb | "has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds" |
| 2 | Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | 7 | occupants | "The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants" |
| 3 | Passengers permitted on board | 6 | passengers | "is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board" |

All three are ceilings ("not more than"); the values given are the maximums permitted, inclusive.

## Interpretation of "occupants it may be authorized to carry" (ask 2)
This is a BasicMed-specific cap applied to the aircraft's authorization: the aircraft's design approval (type certificate, STC, or amended TC — or its operating limitations for experimental aircraft) must authorize no more than 7 occupants, per AC 68-1A sec. 5.1.2 (which describes the same test at the older 6-occupant figure). An aircraft type-certificated for more than 7 occupants does not qualify for BasicMed even if fewer seats are installed or fewer people are aboard; it would require a new design approval (STC/ATC) lowering the authorized occupancy. So the value is 7 occupants authorized, not the aircraft's actual seating or actual load on a given flight.

## Occupant vs. passenger arithmetic (internal consistency check)
The FR preamble is explicit: "a covered aircraft may now be authorized to carry up to 7 occupants (including any required flightcrewmembers) and may be operating with up to 6 passengers on board." Thus 7 authorized occupants = 6 passengers + 1 PIC (or, in a two-pilot-required aircraft, 5 passengers + 2 required flightcrew, still within 7 total occupants). The passenger figure (6) never exceeds the occupant figure (7): 6 ≤ 7 − 1 required crew. Any combination used operationally must satisfy both: total occupants ≤ 7 and passengers ≤ 6.

## Additional operating limits of 61.113(i)(2)–(3) (context only, not among the three asks)
- No flight (or any portion) above 18,000 ft MSL.
- No indicated airspeed exceeding 250 knots.
- No flight outside the United States unless authorized by the country where conducted.
- Not a transport category rotorcraft certified under 14 CFR part 29.
- No carriage of passengers or property for compensation or hire.
- Pilot must have in the logbook the completed CMEC (sec. 68.7) and the BasicMed course completion certificate; must hold a valid U.S. driver's license and meet 61.23(c)(3).

## Superseded guidance — do not use
AC 68-1A (5/3/17) sec. 3.2/5.2.1, the July/Aug 2017 FAA Safety Briefing, and the BasicMed quick-reference card state 5 passengers / 6,000 lb / 6 occupants. Those reflect FESSA sec. 2307 as originally enacted in 2016. Section 828 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 raised the occupant cap 6→7 and the MTOW cap 6,000→12,500 lb, raised the passenger cap 5→6, and added the part 29 rotorcraft exclusion; these were "immediately adopted" in 49 U.S.C. 44703 note and codified in 61.113(i)(1) by the 2024-11-18 final rule. The 2025 CFR annual edition confirms the new text is in force. Only 12,500 lb / 7 occupants / 6 passengers is current.

## Note on "certificated" wording
The FAA web page says "maximum certificated takeoff weight"; the regulation text says "maximum takeoff weight" because experimental aircraft (not type certificated) may also be operated under BasicMed — per the 2024 final rule preamble, the word "certificated" was deliberately omitted from the regulatory text. Either way the numeric ceiling is 12,500 pounds.

## Final answers
1. Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 lb (maximum certificated/maximum takeoff weight, not to exceed).
2. Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7.
3. Passengers on board: 6.

Editorial Note on Part 395




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.


Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:




(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:




(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or






(2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.








(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or





(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.

verdict.summary:
PASSENGER-CARRYING CMV HOURS OF SERVICE — FEDERAL ANSWER

Governing rule: 49 CFR 395.5, 'Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles' (quoted: 70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005; current eCFR and 2025 CFR vol. 5 text agree). Assumptions stated up front, because they are load-bearing: interstate operation, driver of a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach/bus), no exemption under 395.1 applies, and no state intrastate rule is layered on top.

DIRECT ANSWERS

1) Driving limit — 10 hours.
   395.5(a)(1): no driver may drive a passenger-carrying CMV 'more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.' This is a per-duty-period cap: 10 hours of driving, total, within the duty period.

2) Consecutive off-duty time — 8 consecutive hours.
   395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2) both key off '8 consecutive hours off duty.' Eight consecutive hours off duty is what resets the 10-hour driving clock and the 15-hour on-duty clock and starts a new driving period. It must be consecutive; it need not be sleeper-berth time, and the property-carrier 10-hour and split-sleeper-berth constructs in 395.1(g) do not apply here.

3) On-duty limit — 15 hours.
   395.5(a)(2): no driving 'for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.' This is an elapsed on-duty window, not a cap on hours spent driving: once the 15th hour of on-duty time is reached, driving is prohibited even if some of the 10 driving hours remain unused. Coming on duty starts the window; off-duty time inside the window does not pause it.

So the operative triplet for a passenger carrier is 10 / 8 / 15 — ten hours driving, after eight consecutive hours off duty, and no driving after fifteen hours on duty.

SECOND, CUMULATIVE BAR (must be stated or the answer is incomplete)

395.5(b) independently prohibits driving 'regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services' after:
  (b)(1) 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days, if the employing carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
  (b)(2) 70 hours on duty in any period of 8 consecutive days, if the employing carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.
Which of 60/7 or 70/8 applies is a property of the carrier's operating schedule, not the driver's choice; the driver must know which cycle the carrier is on. These caps count on-duty hours (driving plus other on-duty time), not driving hours, and they bar driving even when the 10-hour and 15-hour limits are otherwise satisfied. They are cumulative across carriers.

WHAT DOES *NOT* APPLY (the usual sources of error)

- No 14-hour window. The 14-hour on-duty window is the property-carrying rule (395.3(a)(2)). Passenger carriers get 15 hours under 395.5(a)(2).
- No 11-hour driving limit. That is 395.3(a)(1), property-carrying. Passenger carriers get 10 hours under 395.5(a)(1).
- No 30-minute break requirement. The 395.3(a)(3)(ii) break applies to property-carrying CMVs; it is not imposed on passenger-carrying drivers by 395.5.
- No 10-consecutive-hours-off reset. Ten consecutive hours off duty is the property-carrier reset (395.3(a)(1)); the passenger-carrier reset is 8 consecutive hours (395.5(a)(1)-(2)). The 395.1 short-haul provision quoted in the record confirms the same split — 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty for property-carrying, 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty for passenger-carrying — i.e., the passenger figure is consistently the shorter one.

EXCEPTIONS THAT CAN MOVE THESE NUMBERS (flagged, not applied)

The limits in 395.5 are expressly '[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in 395.1.' Relevant ones a compliance reviewer must check before relying on 10/8/15:
- Adverse driving conditions (395.1(b)): relieves the driving-time limit for the time needed to finish the run, subject to the rule's stated cap; it does not relieve the weekly 60/70-hour caps, and it does not extend the 15-hour on-duty window.
- State-specific rules in 395.1 (e.g., Alaska and Hawaii provisions quoted in the record, which set different driving/on-duty/weekly figures for drivers operating in those states).
- Short-haul / 100 air-mile and other 395.1 exemptions, which can remove record-of-duty-status obligations and, in some cases, the limits themselves.
- Intrastate operations: states adopt their own versions of Part 395; a purely intrastate motorcoach run is governed by the state's rules, which may differ from 10/8/15.

COMPLIANCE / RECORDKEEPING NOTES

- Duty status is recorded for each 24-hour period (395.8(a)(1)); motorcoach operations subject to Part 395 must use an ELD (395.8(a)(1)(i)), with the narrow manual-RODS exceptions in 395.8(a)(1)(ii) (e.g., not more than 8 days of RODS in any 30-day period).
- Carriers retain RODS and supporting documents for at least 6 months (395.8(k)(1)).
- Where a driver is used by more than one carrier in a 24-hour period, the driver submits a RODS to each carrier covering all duty time for the period and naming each carrier (395.8(j)(1)); carriers using a driver for the first time or intermittently must obtain the signed statement of total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time last relieved from duty (395.8(j)(2)). This is how the 60/70-hour cumulative caps are actually verified.

WORKED CHECK (how an auditor applies it)

Driver comes on duty 06:00 after 8+ consecutive hours off duty.
- Driving must stop at 16:00 (10 hours driving) at the latest — and earlier if 10 driving hours are consumed first.
- All driving must stop at 21:00 (15 hours on duty) regardless of remaining driving hours; 2 hours of driving left at 21:00 cannot be used.
- If, before either clock expires, the driver's cumulative on-duty time reaches 60 hours in 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day) or 70 hours in 8 consecutive days (carrier operating every day), driving stops at that moment instead.
- Driving may resume only after 8 consecutive hours off duty, and only if the weekly cap is not exceeded.

BOTTOM LINE: 10 hours of driving, following 8 consecutive hours off duty, and no driving after 15 hours on duty — plus the 60-hour/7-day or 70-hour/8-day cumulative cap, whichever cycle the carrier operates.

verdict.summary:
# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR 135.273(b)

## Holding

| Ask | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Minimum rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **9 consecutive hours** | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2. Lowest rest to which that may be reduced | **8 consecutive hours**, and only on the condition in (b)(3) | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

Both are regulatory minimums. They are floors, not targets, and the operator's operations manual, a collective bargaining agreement, or a customer/contract requirement may impose more; where the operator's own documents are stricter, the stricter number controls as a matter of the operator's compliance with its approved manual.

## 1. Operative regulatory text

14 CFR 135.273(b) (current text, as quoted from eCFR and the GPO CFR volume):

> **(b)(1)** Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours.
>
> **(b)(2)** Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
>
> **(b)(3)** The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Backstops that make the minimum enforceable:

> **(b)(10)** No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section.
>
> **(b)(11)** No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period.

So the rest is owed; the reduction is an election the certificate holder makes in scheduling, not an entitlement the crewmember can waive and not something that can be applied retroactively after the fact.

## 2. Applicability gate — confirm before relying on these numbers

Section 135.273 governs flight attendants; it is not the flight-crewmember rule. Part 135 does not, by itself, force a flight attendant onto every aircraft, so the threshold question is whether the person is a flight attendant required for the flight under the certificate holder's operations specifications (or is assigned as one by the operator). Confirmation steps for the operator:

1. Check the OpSpecs and the aircraft's certification/configuration basis for the requirement to carry a flight attendant on the types flown.
2. Confirm the individual is serving in a flight-attendant capacity, not as a pilot or other crewmember — if the person is a flight crewmember, 135.267 applies instead (see §6 below), and the numbers are different.
3. Confirm the current version of 135.273 in effect on the date of the flight, plus any exemption, waiver, or deviation the certificate holder holds.

If no flight attendant is required or assigned, 135.273 does not apply at all and the two values above are not the governing limits. The request stipulates a flight attendant, so the answer above stands on that premise.

## 3. How to apply it — scheduling procedure

1. **Fix the duty period.** Determine the *scheduled* duty period for the flight attendant (the published/planned duty period, not the post-hoc actual). If the scheduled duty period is 14 hours or less, (b)(2) applies.
2. **Assign the baseline rest.** Schedule at least **9 consecutive hours** of rest, positioned so it falls entirely between completion of the scheduled duty period and the start of the next duty period.
3. **Decide whether to reduce.** If the operation needs the crewmember back sooner, the certificate holder may schedule or reduce that rest to **8 consecutive hours**, but only by simultaneously scheduling the (b)(3) make-up rest.
4. **Build the make-up rest into the same pairing/rotation.** The subsequent rest must be at least **10 consecutive hours**, must begin no later than **24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period**, and must itself fall between completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the following duty period.
5. **Verify continuity.** Count only uninterrupted time free of all duty. Any duty — a flight, positioning/deadhead, training, administrative work, or a required standby/reserve obligation — breaks the period and voids the compliance.
6. **Record it.** Capture scheduled duty period, actual duty period, rest start/end, and (where reduced) the make-up rest start/end in the duty-and-rest records, so the 24-hour test in (b)(3) can be audited.

## 4. The reduction condition, unpacked

The 8-hour figure is lawful only if **all four** elements of (b)(3) are satisfied:

- **Floor:** the reduced rest is **8 consecutive hours** — never 7, never 8 hours broken by a phone call, a van ride counted as duty, or a training module. "Reduced to 8" is the bottom.
- **Compensatory amount:** the subsequent rest is **at least 10 consecutive hours** (more than the 9-hour baseline and more than the 8 hours given, which is the point — the crewmember is repaid).
- **Deadline:** that subsequent rest must **begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period**. The clock starts at the *beginning* of the reduced rest (i.e., at completion of the duty period that preceded it), not at its end.
- **Placement:** that subsequent rest must fall **between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period** — it cannot be pushed past the start of the next duty period or banked for later in the rotation.

Failure of any element converts what looks like a legal 8-hour layover into a violation of (b)(2) (and of (b)(10)).

## 5. Worked example (single time zone, for arithmetic only)

Duty period ends 21:00 Tuesday; the crew is next needed early Wednesday.

- **Baseline (no reduction):** 9 consecutive hours of rest from 21:00 Tue → next duty may commence no earlier than **06:00 Wed**.
- **Reduced:** 8 consecutive hours from 21:00 Tue → next duty may commence **05:00 Wed**, but now the (b)(3) make-up rest is owed. It must begin no later than **21:00 Wed** (24 hours after 21:00 Tue, the beginning of the reduced rest) and must be at least 10 consecutive hours. If Wednesday's duty runs 05:00–19:00 (14 hours, the (b)(1) ceiling), the make-up rest begins at 19:00 Wed — inside the 21:00 Wed deadline — and runs to **05:00 Thu**. Compliant.
- **Non-compliant variant:** if Wednesday's duty runs 05:00–22:00, the make-up rest cannot begin until 22:00 Wed, which is after the 21:00 Wed deadline, so the 8-hour reduction was not available in the first place. The scheduler's only lawful option was the 9-hour baseline (next duty 06:00 Wed).

Practical scheduling consequence: an 8-hour reduction buys one hour in the morning and costs an earlier release (and a 10-hour block) the next day. It should be modeled in the pairing build, not improvised on the day.

## 6. Regimes that are expressly *not* the answer

- **Flight crewmembers (pilots):** 135.267 governs. Its daily limits and rest provisions are separate (e.g., 10 consecutive hours of rest in the 24 hours preceding planned completion; a 16-hour rest after certain exceedances; different reduction mechanics). Do not apply pilot rest numbers to a flight attendant or vice versa.
- **Flight attendant duty periods over 14 hours:** (b)(4)–(b)(6) allow scheduled duty up to 16, 18, or 20 hours only with additional flight attendants assigned (and, for the 18–20 hour case, flights landing/taking off outside the 48 contiguous states and D.C.). Those duty periods carry **12 consecutive hours** of rest under (b)(7), reducible to **10 consecutive hours** under (b)(8) with a subsequent rest of at least **14 consecutive hours** beginning within 24 hours of the reduced rest, and (b)(9) then bars scheduling that flight attendant for more than 14 hours of duty in the 24 hours beginning with the reduced rest. None of that applies to a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, and (b)(9)'s 14-hour cap attaches by its terms to the (b)(8) reduction only — not to a (b)(3) 8-hour reduction.
- **Delays that push actual duty past 14 hours:** the rest provisions key to the *scheduled* duty period, so the governing rest is determined by the schedule, but the crewmember still may not be assigned the next duty period without the minimum rest required by the section (b)(10). If the operator re-schedules or extends a duty period so that it is in fact a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours, the (b)(4)–(b)(9) analysis (additional flight attendants, 12/10-hour rest) is triggered and the 9/8 answer no longer governs. Where actual duty is unexpectedly extended, the conservative and audit-defensible practice is to give at least the greater rest the situation would have required and to document why.
- **Standby/reserve, deadhead, and multi-time-zone measurement:** these affect how the duty period and the rest period are counted (rest must be free of all duty, including positioning), but they do not change the two numbers in this answer. Apply the definitions in 135.273(a) and the operator's manual, and measure the 24-hour deadline in (b)(3) in elapsed time, not local clock time, when the rotation crosses zones.

## 7. Compliance checks (the errors this rule actually produces)

1. Applying the pilot 10-hour/8-hour rest figures to a flight attendant.
2. Scheduling 8 hours without scheduling the 10-hour make-up rest, or scheduling it but placing it after the next duty period begins.
3. Measuring the 24-hour deadline from the *end* of the reduced rest instead of its beginning — that overstates the window by the length of the rest and is the single most common arithmetic error.
4. Counting a reduced rest that is interrupted by a company call, a required check-in, a training assignment, or a positioning leg — (b)(11) forbids any duty during required rest, and an interrupted rest is not "consecutive."
5. Treating the 8-hour reduction as automatic or crewmember-elective rather than a documented scheduling election with the make-up rest built into the same rotation.
6. Letting a delay silently convert a ≤14-hour scheduled duty into a >14-hour one without re-running the (b)(4)–(b)(9) analysis.

## 8. Records and manual integration

- Record, per flight attendant and per duty period: scheduled duty start/end, actual duty start/end, rest start/end, and — for reduced rest — make-up rest start/end and the computed 24-hour deadline. Retain per the certificate holder's FAA-accepted recordkeeping system (see 14 CFR 135.63 and the OpSpecs/manual provisions that implement it).
- The operations manual (and any flight-attendant handbook or CBA) should state the 9-hour baseline, the 8-hour reduction, and the four (b)(3) conditions verbatim in substance, so schedulers are not working from memory. If the manual or CBA sets 10 hours or bars reductions, that stricter standard governs the operator's own compliance.
- Train schedulers and crew tracking on the 24-hour-from-*beginning* test, and configure the crew-management system to hard-block an 8-hour layover unless the make-up rest is present in the rotation and lands inside the window.

## 9. Limits of this answer

These are the regulatory minimums under 135.273 as quoted above, for a flight attendant subject to that section. They do not resolve: whether a flight attendant is required on a specific aircraft/OpSpec (verifiable from the certificate holder's OpSpecs); any exemption, waiver, or deviation held by the operator; the terms of any CBA or manual that may be stricter; or how a specific rotation's duty and rest periods are measured under 135.273(a) definitions and the operator's manual. Each of those should be confirmed against the operator's own documents before the numbers are published in a schedule or a manual.

- Canonical locations: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113 , https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ , https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113

Supporting quotation from the RFC 9113 front matter (as fetched):

> RFC: 9113
> Obsoletes: 7540, 8740
> Category: Standards Track
> Published: June 2022
> ISSN: 2070-1721

and from the abstract:

> This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2). ... This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740.

RFC 9113 replaced RFC 7540 (May 2015, Belshe et al.), which had been the original HTTP/2 specification; the RFC 7540 text itself notes only that it "is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax." RFC 9113 is a revision of the HTTP/2 protocol, not a new protocol version: the ALPN identifiers `h2`/`h2c`, the PRI method, and the frame type / settings / error code registries established by RFC 7540 carry over, and RFC 9113's Section 11 states that IANA updated the references to RFC 7540 in those registries to point to RFC 9113.

## 2. What RFC 9113 obsoletes

Exactly two RFCs, per the document's own `Obsoletes` header and its abstract:

| Obsoleted RFC | Title / role | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **RFC 7540** | *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)*, May 2015 | The original HTTP/2 specification; wholly replaced. |
| **RFC 8740** | *Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2* | Its TLS 1.3 usage is folded into RFC 9113; Appendix B states: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes." |

## 3. Scope decisions and exclusions (stated explicitly)

1. **"Current" = as of the lookup timestamp.** The evidence was fetched 2026-11-17T05:30Z from rfc-editor.org and datatracker.ietf.org. If a later RFC supersedes RFC 9113, this answer changes; re-verify with the procedure in §4.
2. **"Obsoletes" = direct obsoletion only**, i.e. the RFC's own `Obsoletes:` header / abstract / Appendix B statement. Indirect chains (e.g. an RFC that obsoleted something RFC 9113 in turn obsoletes) are out of scope.
3. **Errata are not obsoletions.** Errata against RFC 9113 may exist; they correct text and do not create or remove an `Obsoletes` relationship. Nothing in the answer depends on errata status.
4. **Not obsoleted by RFC 9113** (common confusions to avoid):
   - **RFC 7541** (*HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2*) — still a separate, current specification; RFC 9113 references it, does not obsolete it.
   - **RFC 9110 / RFC 9111 / RFC 9112** (*HTTP Semantics* / *HTTP Caching* / *HTTP/1.1*) — sibling documents in the same 2022 HTTP revision; not obsoleted by RFC 9113.
   - **RFC 9218** (*Extensible Prioritization Scheme for HTTP*) — RFC 9113 *deprecates* the RFC 7540 priority scheme and recommends RFC 9218, but does not obsolete any RFC by that act.
5. **"Deprecated" ≠ "obsoleted."** RFC 9113 deprecates the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism (and with it the `HTTP2-Settings` header field and the `h2c` upgrade token, both defined in RFC 7540) and deprecates the RFC 7540 priority scheme. These are feature-level deprecations inside the protocol, not RFC-level obsoletions; they add no RFC to the §2 list.

## 4. Re-verification procedure (how to confirm or refute this answer)

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ and read the metadata block. Confirm `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`.
2. On the same page confirm the **"Obsoleted by"** field is *empty* / absent. A non-empty "Obsoleted by" means RFC 9113 is no longer current — stop and report the new RFC number instead.
3. Cross-check https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ for status (e.g. any `draft-ietf-httpbis-*` successor that has reached RFC) and for the "Obsoletes"/"Obsoleted by" relation fields.
4. Read the RFC 9113 abstract and Appendix B in the published text for the normative prose sentence ("This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740.") — the header and the prose must agree; if they disagree, the header plus the RFC Editor's index entry governs.
5. Optional secondary check: RFC Editor index search for "HTTP/2" and for RFC 7540 — the RFC 7540 entry should list RFC 9113 in its "Obsoleted by" field.

## 5. One-line citation-ready form

> The current specification of HTTP/2 is RFC 9113 (Standards Track, June 2022), which obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.

Explanatory Note
(This note is not part of the Regulations)
These Regulations amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (“the 2015 Regulations”) (S.I. 2015/621). These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.
Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (regulation 4 of the 2015 Regulations).
Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
Regulation 2(3)(b) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are under the age of 18 from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(c) of the 2015 Regulations).

Impact Assessments generally accompany all UK Government interventions of a regulatory nature that affect the private sector, civil society organisations and public services. They apply regardless of whether the regulation originates from a domestic or international source and can accompany primary (Acts etc) and secondary legislation (SIs). An Impact Assessment allows those with an interest in the policy area to understand:
Why the government is proposing to intervene;
The main options the government is considering, and which one is preferred;
How and to what extent new policies may impact on them; and,
The estimated costs and benefits of proposed measures.

quotes.whole:
This year, in addition to the NLW increase, the Government will implement an above-inflation increase to the Universal Credit standard allowance, which will further boost household incomes for many NLW workers.
We expect NLW coverage (the number of jobs paid up to 5 pence above the NLW) to fall this year to around 5.9 per cent of jobs.
Youth Rates of the National Minimum Wage
The 18-20 Year Old Rate increases by 8.5 per cent in April to reach £10.85. Our recommendations for this age group balanced labour market conditions with the Government’s commitment, as stated in our 2025 remit, to reduce and eventually eliminate the difference between the NLW and the 18-20 Year Old Rate. The 18-20 Year Old Rate is now at 85 per cent of the NLW rate – a similar proportion to the early years of the NMW.
The 16-17 Year Old Rate and the Apprentice Rate will increase by 6 per cent to £8.00 in April. These increases ensure that pay for these workers does not become too detached from the rates for older workers.
As a result of these increases we expect youth coverage to rise. However, the impacts on effective coverage (the number of jobs paid below the NLW) are more uncertain.
Our remit for 2026

quotes.whole:
A lot has changed since we gave our advice to the Government last autumn, and we are now beginning to gather evidence for recommendations later this year. The current economic uncertainty makes it essential that the Commission hears from those affected by the minimum wage and builds consensus for evidence-based recommendations.
To mark the uprating, the Low Pay Commission has published a report looking at the immediate impacts of the new rates. It has also published a consultation to inform its recommendations on future minimum wage rates.
NOTES FOR EDITORS
The LPC’s recommendations were submitted to the Government on 27 October 2025. The Government announced acceptance of those recommendations at the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 26 November.
The Government’s remit to the LPC, which determines the Commission’s work through the year, was published on 16 March and is available here.
The National Living Wage (NLW) is currently the statutory minimum wage for workers aged 21 and over. This age threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024.

verdict.summary:
UK statutory minimum wage rates effective 1 April 2026

ANSWERS
1) National Living Wage (workers aged 21 and over): £12.71 per hour, from 1 April 2026. (Up from £12.21; +£0.50, +4.1%.)
2) National Minimum Wage, 18–20 Year Old Rate: £10.85 per hour, from 1 April 2026. (Up from £10.00; +£0.85, +8.5%.)

Both are gross hourly pay rates, UK-wide (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland). The National Living Wage is the statutory rate set under the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 — it is not the voluntary 'UK Living Wage' / 'Real Living Wage' published by the Living Wage Foundation, which is a separate, higher, non-statutory figure.

FULL 2026 RATE TABLE (context; the two answers above are the first two rows)
| Band | Rate from 1 Apr 2026 | Previous (to 31 Mar 2026) | Change (£) | Change (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £12.21 | +0.50 | 4.1 |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £10.00 | +0.85 | 8.5 |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | +0.45 | 6.0 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | +0.45 | 6.0 |
| Accommodation Offset (daily limit) | £11.10 | £10.66 | +0.44 | 4.1 |

EFFECTIVE DATE AND LEGAL BASIS
- Effective date: rates apply to pay reference periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026. The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 come into force on 1 April 2026 and extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
- The instrument amends the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (S.I. 2015/621): reg. 2(2) substitutes '£12.71' for '£12.21' in reg. 4 (national living wage); reg. 2(3)(a) substitutes '£10.85' for '£10.00' in reg. 4A(1)(b) (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21); reg. 2(3)(b)/(c) substitute '£8.00' for '£7.55' in reg. 4A(1)(c)/(d) (under 18 and apprentice); reg. 2(4) substitutes '£11.10' for '£10.66' in reg. 16(1) (accommodation offset).
- Status: the rates are settled, not provisional. The Low Pay Commission recommended them on 27 October 2025; the Government accepted the recommendations in full and announced them at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025; the rates were in force from 1 April 2026.

SOURCES (all agree on £12.71 and £10.85)
1. The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (draft SI, laying citation 2026 No., coming into force 1 April 2026) — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukdsi/2026/9780348279030 (primary legislation; see reg. 2 and the Explanatory Note).
2. Low Pay Commission, 'Minimum wage rates for 2026' (published 26 November 2025) — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/minimum-wage-rates-for-2026.
3. GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage rates' (current rates table, April 2026 row) — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates.
4. Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' (published 1 April 2026) — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026; and press release 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour' — https://www.gov.uk/government/news/national-living-wage-increases-to-1271-per-hour.

INTERNAL CONSISTENCY CHECKS (performed)
- 12.71 − 12.21 = 0.50 → 0.50/12.21 = 4.1% ✔ matches the published percentage.
- 10.85 − 10.00 = 0.85 → 0.85/10.00 = 8.5% ✔ matches.
- 10.85 / 12.71 = 85.4%, consistent with the LPC's statement that the 18–20 rate is 'now at 85 per cent of the NLW rate'. ✔
- 8.00 − 7.55 = 0.45 → 6.0% ✔; 11.10 − 10.66 = 0.44 → 4.1% ✔.
- Age-band ordering holds: 12.71 (21+) > 10.85 (18–20) > 8.00 (16–17) = 8.00 (apprentice). ✔

QUALIFICATIONS TO CARRY WITH ANY USE OF THESE FIGURES
- Age is determined by the worker's age in the pay reference period in which the work is done, not by the date of hiring.
- An apprentice aged 19+ who has completed the first year of their apprenticeship is entitled to the rate for their age (e.g. £12.71 if 21+), not the apprentice rate; the apprentice rate applies to apprentices under 19, or 19+ in the first year.
- The accommodation offset (£11.10 per day from 1 April 2026) reduces the cash minimum wage an employer may count when accommodation is provided; it does not change the headline hourly rates above.
- Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland use the same UK-wide statutory rates; there is no devolved variation in the NMW/NLW hourly figures.

quotes.whole:
What has changed?
Short-haul Exception
Expands the short-haul exception to 150 air-miles and allows a 14-hour work shift to take place as part of the exception.
Adverse Driving Conditions Exception
Expands the driving window during adverse driving conditions by up to an additional 2 hours.
30-Minute Break Requirement
Requires break of at least 30 consecutive minutes after 8 cumulative hours of driving time (instead of on-duty time) and allows an on-duty/not driving period to qualify as the required break.
Sleeper Berth Provision
Modifies the sleeper berth exception to allow a driver to meet the 10-hour minimum off-duty requirement by spending at least 7 hours of that period in the berth combined with a minimum off-duty period of at least 2 hours spent inside or outside the berth, provided the two periods total at least 10 hours. When used together as specified, neither qualify period counts against the 14-hour driving window.
Educational Tool for Hours of Service (ETHOS)
FMCSA launched a new online tool that allows users to enter driver records of duty status to see if there are potential violations with the new hours of service regulations.

Who Must Comply?
Most commercial motor vehicle (CMV) drivers must comply. In general, a CMV is a vehicle that is used as part of a business and is involved in interstate commerce and fits any of these descriptions:
Weighs 10,001 pounds or more
Has a gross vehicle weight rating or gross combination weight rating of 10,001 pounds or more
Is designed or used to transport 16 or more passengers (including the driver) not for compensation
Is designed or used to transport 9 or more passengers (including the driver) for compensation
Is transporting hazardous materials in a quantity requiring placards

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1))

ANSWERS
1. Radius: 150 air miles (the regulation's own parenthetical conversion: 172.6 statute miles) from the normal work reporting location. — 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i)
2. Release: the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. — 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii)

CONTROLLING TEXT (current eCFR, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), fetched 2026-11-17)
"(e) Short-haul operations — (1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
(iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
(B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
(iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) total hours on-duty each day; (C) time released from duty each day; and (D) total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

RULE VERSION PIN
These figures are the post-2020 HOS final rule values (compliance date 29 September 2020), which raised the short-haul radius from 100 to 150 air miles and the duty period from 12 to 14 hours. Any citation to a pre-2020 edition (100 air miles / 12 hours) is superseded and must not be used.

SCOPE AND VARIANTS
- The 150/14 pair in (e)(1) applies to both property-carrying and passenger-carrying CMV drivers. The only difference is the intervening off-duty period: 10 consecutive hours for property-carrying, 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying. Both variants carry the same 150 air-mile radius and the same 14-consecutive-hour release.
- Do not confuse this with § 395.1(e)(2), the non-CDL property-carrying provision: it also uses a 150 air-mile radius, but it requires return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour and caps driving at the 14th hour on 5 of 7 days and the 16th hour on 2 of 7 days. It is not a flat "released within 14 consecutive hours" rule and does not answer this question.
- Driver-salespersons: the return-and-release condition in (e)(1)(ii) is expressly inapplicable to a driver-salesperson; the 150 air-mile radius condition in (e)(1)(i) still applies.

WHAT THE EXCEPTION DOES AND DOES NOT RELIEVE
- Relieved: the records-of-duty-status requirement (§ 395.8) and the ELD requirement (§ 395.11). Qualifying drivers also are not required to take the 30-minute break under § 395.1(e)(1).
- Not relieved: the substantive driving and on-duty limits of § 395.3 (11-hour driving limit, 14-hour driving window for property carriers, 60/70-hour limit) remain in force. Note the interaction for passenger carriers: § 395.3 permits 15 hours on duty, but a passenger-carrying driver claiming (e)(1) must still be released within 14 consecutive hours, so the exception is the tighter constraint.

MEASUREMENT AND VERIFICATION PROCEDURE
1. Fix the normal work reporting location for the duty tour — the location where the driver reports to and is released from work. Per FMCSA guidance, this location may differ from shift to shift provided the driver starts and ends each shift at the same location.
2. Measure the radius as a straight-line (great-circle) distance in air miles — 1 air mile = 1 nautical mile = 1.15078 statute miles — from that location to the farthest point the vehicle reaches during the tour. 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles. Do not use route/driving distance; the regulation measures air miles, and the statute-mile figure is only the converted equivalent.
3. Measure the 14 hours from the moment the driver comes on duty (report time) to the moment the carrier releases the driver from duty at the work reporting location. Both events — the return and the release — must fall inside the same 14-consecutive-hour window. Off-duty time inside the tour does not extend that window.
4. Evidence file per driver-day: report time, total hours on duty, release time, and total time for the preceding 7 days for new or intermittent drivers. Retain 6 months.

FALLBACK / TRIGGERS (exception forfeited for the day)
- The driver exceeds 150 air miles from the normal work reporting location at any point in the tour, or
- the driver is not returned to that location and released within 14 consecutive hours, or
- the required off-duty period (10 hours property / 8 hours passenger) is not taken between tours.
On any of these, the driver must complete a record of duty status for that day (paper log or ELD) and the carrier must retain it; the time-record substitute is no longer sufficient. Adverse driving conditions do not cure a missed 14-hour release — FMCSA's guidance is that a short-haul driver who cannot return within 14 hours must record duty status for that day. Separately, a driver who has used the short-haul exception on more than 8 days in the last 30 days must use an ELD to record time for that day.

OPEN ITEMS OUTSIDE THIS DETERMINATION
- State-level adaptations and carrier policy may impose shorter windows or smaller radii; this determination states the federal floor only.
- Nothing here addresses Canadian or Mexican analogues.

quotes.whole:
3.1 What Do I Need to Fly Under BasicMed?
1. Hold a current and valid U.S. driver’s license.
2. Hold or have held a medical certificate issued by the FAA at any point after
July 14, 2006.
3. Answer the health questions on the Comprehensive Medical Examination
Checklist (CMEC).
4. Get your physical examination by any State-licensed physician, and have that
physician complete the CMEC (be sure to keep the CMEC).
5. Take the BasicMed online medical education course. Keep the course
completion document issued to you by the course provider.
3.2 What Are My BasicMed Privileges? You can conduct any operation that you would
otherwise be able to conduct using your pilot certificate and a third-class medical
certificate, except you are limited to:
1. Fly with no more than five passengers.
2. Fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than
6,000 lbs.
3. Fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants.
4. Flights within the United States, at an indicated airspeed of 250 knots or less,
and at an altitude at or below 18,000 feet mean sea level (MSL).
5. You may not fly for compensation or hire.

verdict.summary:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT OPERATING LIMITS (US, 14 CFR part 68 / § 61.113(i))

BOTTOM LINE — the three limits, as currently in force:

| Limit | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum takeoff weight | 12,500 lb | 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) |
| Occupants the aircraft may be AUTHORIZED to carry | 7 occupants | 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) |
| Passengers ON BOARD | 6 passengers | 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) |

Plus one categorical exclusion in the same sentence: the aircraft must NOT be a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29.

1. CONTROLLING REGULATORY TEXT

14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) (current eCFR, amended through Amdt. 61-159, 90 FR 35218, July 24, 2025) provides that a private pilot may act as PIC or required flightcrew member without a part 67 medical certificate if the pilot holds a valid U.S. driver's license, meets § 61.23(c)(3), and complies with all of the following conditions and limitations:

  "(1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter; and
   (2) The flight, including each portion of the flight, is not carried out—
     (i) At an altitude that is more than 18,000 feet above mean sea level;
     (ii) Outside the United States unless authorized by the country in which the flight is conducted; or
     (iii) At an indicated airspeed exceeding 250 knots; and
   (3) The pilot has available in his or her logbook—
     (i) The completed medical examination checklist required under § 68.7 of this chapter; and
     (ii) The certificate of course completion required under § 61.23(c)(3)."

FAA corroboration, BasicMed airman page (faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med):
  Aircraft Requirements — "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants"; "Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds."
  Operating Requirements — "Carries not more than six passengers."

Statutory basis: BasicMed was created by § 2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (PL 114-190), implemented through 14 CFR part 68 and § 61.113(i). The aircraft limits above are the expanded figures mandated by § 828 ("Expansion of BasicMed") of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (PL 118-63), effective November 12, 2024.

2. WHAT EACH FIGURE MEANS — AND WHY THE THREE ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE

(a) 12,500 lb — MAXIMUM TAKEOFF WEIGHT. This is the aircraft's maximum (certificated) takeoff weight as established by its design approval — type certificate, supplemental type certificate, or amended TC — or, for experimental aircraft issued a special airworthiness certificate, as determined in the operating limitations established by the operator. It is a hard ceiling: the aircraft's MTOW must be 12,500 lb or less. If an aircraft was certificated above 12,500 lb and is altered (via STC/ATC) to a maximum certificated takeoff weight of 12,500 lb or less, it then qualifies. Note that § 61.113(i)(1) does not relieve the aircraft from its own operating limitations; where an operating limitation is more restrictive, the more restrictive limitation governs.

(b) 7 OCCUPANTS — AUTHORIZED OCCUPANCY. This is a property of the AIRCRAFT, not of the flight: the number of occupants the aircraft is AUTHORIZED to carry under federal law (design approval, or the operating limitations for experimental aircraft). It includes the pilot and any required flightcrew. An aircraft whose approval authorizes 8 or more occupants does not qualify at all, regardless of how many people actually get in. An aircraft type-certificated for more than 7 occupants may be made eligible by alteration under a new design approval (STC or ATC) that reduces authorized occupancy to 7 or fewer.

(c) 6 PASSENGERS — ACTUAL LOAD. This is a property of the FLIGHT: the number of passengers actually on board may not exceed 6. Read together with (b):
  - Single-pilot-certificated aircraft: 1 pilot + up to 6 passengers = 7 occupants — the maximum use of both limits.
  - Two-pilot-certificated aircraft (two required flightcrew): 2 required pilots + up to 5 passengers = 7 occupants.
  - Occupants other than the PIC operating under BasicMed may be passengers, required pilot flightcrew members, or a flight instructor giving instruction; a non-required pilot who is neither required flightcrew nor an instructor providing instruction counts as a passenger.

So: 7 is the certification-side ceiling (who the aircraft may carry), 6 is the operations-side ceiling (who is actually carried). Both must be satisfied on every flight; satisfying one does not excuse the other.

3. IMPORTANT — SUPERSEDED FIGURES TO NOT USE

The pre-November 12, 2024 limits were: 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight, aircraft authorized to carry not more than 6 occupants, and not more than 5 passengers on board. Those figures still appear in:
  - FAA Advisory Circular AC 68-1A (5/3/17), §§ 3.2, 5.1.1, 5.1.3, 5.2.1 (6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers);
  - FAA Advisory Circular AC 68-1 (1/9/17) (same);
  - the printed 2024 edition of 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) on govinfo (6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers);
  - FAA Notice N 8000.386, which recites them as the "before" set.
They are obsolete. Notice N 8000.386 (11/14/24) states the transition explicitly: "Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024: The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, The aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and The aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board." Any answer using 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers is out of date for flights on or after 11/12/2024.

4. PRACTITIONER NOTES / VERIFICATION ITEMS

- These three aircraft limits are only one element of BasicMed eligibility. The other conditions — at or below 18,000 ft MSL, within the US (or a country where BasicMed is authorized), indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots, no compensation or hire, plus the driver's license, prior-medical-after-7/14/2006, CMEC, physician exam, and online course requirements — are outside the scope of this question but operate cumulatively. An aircraft that meets 12,500 lb / 7 occupants / 6 passengers can still be flown outside BasicMed's privileges if any of the other conditions is breached.
- 14 CFR § 91.319(j) governs experimental aircraft operated under BasicMed and historically mirrored the occupant ceiling. The version of § 91.319(j) quoted in the 2017 ACs reflects the pre-expansion six-occupant figure; the current text should be checked against eCFR before relying on a specific number for experimental aircraft. The rule of construction is that the experimental aircraft's special airworthiness operating limitations control, and they cannot be more permissive than § 61.113(i)(1).
- Verification: confirm the current text of § 61.113(i)(1) and § 91.319(j) on eCFR before each use, since the part 61 amendment history shows frequent changes (most recently Amdt. 61-158, 89 FR 90577, 11/18/2024 and Amdt. 61-159, 90 FR 35218, 7/24/2025).

quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 395




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.


Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:




(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:




(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or






(2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.








(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or





(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.





[70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005]

More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty, or

No motor carrier of passengers shall permit or require any passenger-carrying CMV driver to drive, regardless of number of motor carriers using the driver’s services, for any period after the driver has been on duty:

Off-Duty Time
“Off-duty time” is not speciﬁcally deﬁned in the regulations. In effect, it is any time that is not “driving time,” “on-duty time,” or “sleeper berth” as deﬁned in § 395.2.
The following guidelines must be met before a driver is considered off duty for meal and other routine stops made during a work shift:
The driver must be relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the bus or passenger-carrying CMV, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage and freight that it may be transporting.

quotes.whole:
On-Duty Time – § 395.2
On-duty time means all time from the time a driver begins work or is required to be in readiness for work until the time the driver is relieved from work and all responsibilities for performing work. Performing other compensated work for a person who is not a motor
carrier is also on-duty time. The complete deﬁnition of on-duty time can be found in § 395.2.
Travel Time – § 395.1(j)
When a driver at the direction of a motor carrier is traveling, but not driving any vehicle or assuming any other responsibility to the carrier (“cushioning”), such time shall be counted as on-duty time unless the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty when arriving at destination, in which case he/she shall be
considered off duty for the entire period.
Relief Drivers
On long-distance trips requiring straight-through driving, motorcoach companies may send a relief driver ahead.
In cases when the driver is driven or uses public transportation to get to a layover location, and the driver has 8 consecutive hours off duty after arriving, travel time may be recorded as off duty.

Multiple Employer Driver – § 395.8(j)
Some passenger carriers make frequent use of part-time and multiple-employer drivers. When using a driver intermittently, obtain a signed statement from the driver that indicates the total time on duty during the preceding 7 days and the time at which the driver was last relieved from duty prior to using such driver. All compensated work for a motor carrier or a non-motor carrier is on-duty time.
Electronic Logging Device (ELD) Regulations
The ELD regulations apply to most motor carriers of passengers and their drivers who are required to keep a record of duty status. These regulations apply to drivers domiciled in Canada and Mexico when operating within the United States, unless they qualify for an exception.
Exceptions to the ELD Regulations:
Drivers who are required to prepare a record of duty status no more than 8 days during any 30-day period.

verdict.summary:
# Hours of service for a passenger-carrying CMV driver (US federal, interstate)

**Scope of this answer:** current US federal FMCSA hours-of-service rules for a *passenger-carrying* commercial motor vehicle (motorcoach/bus) operated by an interstate motor carrier — 49 CFR Part 395, specifically § 395.5. These are the three per-duty-period limits asked for. Weekly cumulative caps and the exceptions that can move the numbers are noted separately below so they are not confused with the base answers.

## 1. The three answers

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** of driving, following 8 consecutive hours off duty | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8 consecutive hours** off duty | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2) |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive? | **15 hours** on duty, following 8 consecutive hours off duty | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(2) |

Controlling text, § 395.5(a) (verbatim, eCFR):

> "Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1: (a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle: (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."

Note the structure: the 8-hour off-duty period is the *reset* that starts a fresh 10-hour driving allotment and a fresh 15-hour on-duty count. It is **8** consecutive hours for passenger-carrying vehicles, not 10 (10 is the property-carrying figure, § 395.3(a)(1)).

## 2. How the three limits interact

Both per-shift limits run simultaneously; **whichever is reached first stops driving.** Driving is capped at 10 hours, and driving is also prohibited once on-duty time reaches 15 hours, even if fewer than 10 hours have been spent driving. Two consequences that are commonly missed:

- **The 15-hour limit is a cumulative on-duty clock, not an elapsed 15-hour window.** Off-duty time is not counted in the 15-hour period (FMCSA summary for passenger-carrying drivers: "Off-duty time is not included in the 15-hour period"). A mid-shift off-duty break therefore pushes the 15-on-duty-hour point later on the clock. This is the key structural difference from the property-carrying 14-hour window, which off-duty time does *not* extend.
- **Reaching either limit bars driving only, not other work.** After 10 driving hours or 15 on-duty hours the driver may not drive, but the regulation does not by itself forbid continued on-duty non-driving work. Practically, though, that work consumes the 15-hour on-duty budget and must be logged.

## 3. Worked example (shows both limits and the reset)

Driver reports for duty at 06:00.

| Clock | Activity | Cumulative driving | Cumulative on-duty |
|---|---|---|---|
| 06:00–08:00 | Driving | 2.0 | 2.0 |
| 08:00–09:00 | On duty, not driving | 2.0 | 3.0 |
| 09:00–12:00 | Driving | 5.0 | 6.0 |
| 12:00–13:00 | **Off duty** (not counted toward 15) | 5.0 | 6.0 |
| 13:00–17:00 | Driving | 9.0 | 10.0 |
| 17:00–18:00 | On duty, not driving | 9.0 | 11.0 |
| 18:00–19:00 | Driving | **10.0** | 12.0 |

At 19:00 the driver has used exactly 10.0 driving hours (the cap — no further driving) while having accumulated only 12.0 of the 15 on-duty hours. **The 10-hour driving limit binds first.** The driver may not drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty have been taken; going off duty at 19:00, the earliest new driving allotment begins at 03:00 the next day.

Variant showing the 15-hour limit binding: if the same driver had accumulated 15 on-duty hours (e.g., 6 on-duty hours before the 12:00–13:00 off-duty break plus 9 on-duty hours after it, reaching 15 at 22:00 on the clock) with only 8 driving hours, driving would be barred from 22:00 onward by § 395.5(a)(2).

## 4. What counts as on-duty and off-duty (this is what makes the numbers move)

- **On-duty time, § 395.2:** all time from when the driver begins work or is required to be in readiness for work until relieved from work and all responsibility for performing work. It includes waiting time in readiness, loading/unloading and passenger handling, inspection, and **other compensated work for a non-motor-carrier employer**. All compensated work counts.
- **Off-duty time:** not separately defined; in effect, any time that is not driving time, on-duty time, or sleeper-berth time. FMCSA's guidelines require, for meal and routine stops to be off duty, that the driver be **relieved of all duty and responsibility for the care and custody of the bus/CMV, its accessories, and any passengers, baggage and freight it is carrying.** A driver who stays with the coach and remains responsible for passengers is not off duty.
- **Travel/cushioning time, § 395.1(j):** travel at the carrier's direction but not driving and not assuming other responsibility counts as on-duty **unless** the driver is afforded at least 8 consecutive hours off duty on arrival, in which case the whole period may be recorded as off duty. Relief-driver travel to a layover works the same way.

## 5. Exceptions that can lawfully move the three numbers

Apply only by their own terms; do not build them into the baseline.

1. **Adverse driving conditions** — FMCSA's passenger-carrier summary states drivers may extend the 10-hour maximum driving time and the 15-hour on-duty limit by **up to 2 hours** when adverse driving conditions (as defined in § 395.2) are encountered; § 395.1(b) is the operative provision. Verify the current § 395.1(b) text for the exact conditions and any post-run off-duty requirement before relying on it.
2. **Sleeper berth, § 395.1(g)(3)** — a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth (defined in § 393.76) may accumulate the **equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty** by taking two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided the four requirements of § 395.1(g)(3)(i)–(iv) are met. As FMCSA summarizes it: at least 8 hours in the sleeper berth, splittable into two periods **neither less than 2 hours**, and the pairing must total at least 8 hours. Read the subparagraph text before using a split.
3. **Other § 395.1 exemptions** — the regulation is expressly "subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1." If the operation relies on any of them, confirm it by its own terms and keep the supporting documentation.

## 6. What does NOT apply to passenger-carrying drivers (common, expensive error)

These are **property-carrying** rules in § 395.3 and the 2020 flexibility amendments, and they do not set the limits for a motorcoach:

- 11-hour driving limit (§ 395.3(a)(1)) — passenger limit is 10.
- 14-hour driving window (§ 395.3(a)(2)) — passenger limit is 15 on-duty hours, with off-duty time excluded.
- 30-minute break after 8 cumulative driving hours (§ 395.3(a)(3)(ii)) — a property-carrying requirement; it is not part of § 395.5.
- 34-hour restart (§ 395.3(c)) — property-carrying; § 395.5(b) contains no restart provision for passenger carriers.
- The 2-hour/7-hour split of the 10-hour off-duty period — that is the property-carrying sleeper split; the passenger split runs off the 8-hour requirement in § 395.1(g)(3).
- The 150-air-mile short-haul exception in § 395.1(e) is written for property-carrying CMV drivers and does not relieve a passenger-carrying driver of § 395.5.

## 7. Weekly cumulative caps (for completeness — not answers to asks 1–3)

Separately from the per-shift limits, § 395.5(b) bars driving after the driver has been on duty, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services:

- **60 hours in any 7 consecutive days** if the employing carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- **70 hours in any 8 consecutive days** if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.

A passenger carrier may use either cycle. These are cumulative caps, not per-shift limits, and there is no 34-hour restart available under § 395.5.

## 8. "Per day/shift" — no 24-hour reset

The limits attach to a **duty period**, not to a calendar day or a fixed 24-hour window. There is no rule that a driver is refreshed at midnight or after 24 hours; only **8 consecutive hours off duty** starts a new 10-hour/15-hour cycle, and the 60/70-hour caps are measured on rolling 7/8-day periods.

## 9. Jurisdiction caveat

The values above are the **federal** baseline for an interstate carrier. Intrastate-only passenger operations may be governed by state hours-of-service rules (some states, e.g. California, impose their own intrastate limits), and a state may be **stricter** than the federal rule where it applies. Before publishing these numbers as an operating policy, confirm (a) that the carrier is subject to federal rules rather than a state intrastate regime, and (b) whether any state in which the driver operates imposes a lower limit. A stricter state rule would reduce the three values, never raise them.

## 10. Records to support the numbers

Driver's record of duty status under § 395.8 (ELD for most passenger carriers and drivers required to keep RODS), retained **6 months** per § 395.1(e)-style time-record requirements and § 395.8; for multiple-employer/intermittent drivers, a signed statement of total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time last relieved from duty (§ 395.8(j)). Compensated work for any employer counts as on-duty.

## 11. Citations

- 49 CFR § 395.5(a)(1)–(2) — 10 hours driving / 8 consecutive hours off duty; no driving after 15 hours on duty. (70 FR 50073, Aug. 25, 2005; text unchanged in the eCFR snapshot consulted.)
- 49 CFR § 395.5(b)(1)–(2) — 60-hour/7-day and 70-hour/8-day on-duty caps.
- 49 CFR § 395.2 — definitions of on-duty time, driving time, sleeper berth, adverse driving conditions.
- 49 CFR § 395.1(b) (adverse driving conditions), § 395.1(g)(3) (passenger sleeper berth), § 395.1(j) (travel time).
- FMCSA, "Hours of Service — Motor Carriers of Passengers" and "Summary of Hours of Service Regulations" (passenger-carrying column): 10-hour driving limit, 15-hour limit with off-duty time excluded, 60/70-hour limit, sleeper-berth split, +2-hour adverse-conditions relief; off-duty guidelines for meal and routine stops.

**Bottom line:** a motorcoach driver may drive **10 hours** after **8 consecutive hours off duty**, and may not drive after being on duty **15 hours** following those 8 consecutive hours off duty — whichever limit is reached first.

Subpart B—Flight Operations
§ 135.61 General.
This subpart prescribes rules, in addition to those in part 91 of this chapter, that apply to operations under this part.
§ 135.63 Recordkeeping requirements.
(a) Each certificate holder shall keep at its principal business office or at other places approved by the Administrator, and shall make available for inspection by the Administrator the following—

(v) The effective date and class of the medical certificate that the pilot holds.

What are the flight attendant duty period and rest requirements?
In most cases, if you have a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, you must have at least nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest after your duty period before you have another duty period. However, under certain circumstances, our regulations allow a rest period of only eight consecutive hours. If your employer schedules you for an eight hour rest period, your next rest period must be at least 10 consecutive hours and must begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the eight hour rest period.
You can find additional guidance on our Cabin Safety Legal Interpretations website.

verdict.summary:
BOTTOM LINE

Under 14 CFR Part 135, a flight attendant who is scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less must receive a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. That rest may be scheduled at, or reduced to, 8 consecutive hours — but only if the flight attendant is then given a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours that is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period.

| Element | Value | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Rest owed after a scheduled duty period of 14 h or less | 9 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(2) |
| Minimum to which that rest may be reduced | 8 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Compensatory rest triggered by the 8-hour reduction | at least 10 consecutive hours | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Deadline for the compensatory rest to begin | no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period | §135.273(b)(3) |
| Required placement of both rests | between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period | §135.273(b)(2), (b)(3) |

1. THE BASE REQUIREMENT — 9 CONSECUTIVE HOURS

§135.273(b)(1) bars assigning a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours (except under the augmented-crew paragraphs (b)(4)–(b)(6)). §135.273(b)(2) then provides that a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less 'must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours,' which 'must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.' The FAA's published FAQ states the same: with a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, at least nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest is required before the next duty period.

Two points operators routinely get wrong:

- The 9 hours is keyed to the DUTY PERIOD, not to flight time. Unlike the flight-crewmember table in §135.265(b) (9/10/11 hours depending on scheduled flight time), §135.273 imposes a flat 9-hour minimum for any duty period of 14 hours or less. A four-hour duty day still generates 9 hours of rest for a flight attendant covered by §135.273.
- It is 'scheduled rest,' i.e., a rest period built into the assignment. §135.273(b)(10) prohibits assigning a flight attendant to any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section, and (b)(11) prohibits assigning a flight attendant to perform any duty during any required rest period. The regulation does not prescribe where the rest is taken or require a rest facility for flight attendants; it requires consecutive hours free of duty.

2. THE REDUCTION — DOWN TO 8 CONSECUTIVE HOURS, WITH A PRICE

§135.273(b)(3): 'The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'

The reduction is therefore conditional, and all four elements must be satisfied:

(a) The reduced rest is at least 8 consecutive hours — 8 is the floor; (b)(3) authorizes no shorter rest, and there is no provision in §135.273 permitting anything less for a 14-hour-or-less duty period.
(b) A subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours is provided.
(c) That subsequent rest is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period.
(d) Both rests fall between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Note that (b)(3) says 'scheduled or reduced.' The 8-hour rest may be planned in the pairing/crew schedule up front, or the 9-hour rest may be reduced in real time; either path triggers the full compensatory-rest obligation. There is no 'one-time' or 'discretionary' reduction that escapes the 10-hour makeup rest.

Worked timeline. Duty period ends 2100 on Day 1.
- Normal case: 9 consecutive hours of rest, 2100 Day 1 to 0600 Day 2; next duty may report at 0600 Day 2.
- Reduced case: 8 consecutive hours of rest, 2100 Day 1 to 0500 Day 2 (reduced rest begins 2100 Day 1). The subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours must BEGIN no later than 2100 Day 2 (24 hours after 2100 Day 1) and must run between the end of the Day 2 duty period and the start of the next duty period. A Day 2 duty period of 0500–1400 followed by rest beginning 1400 Day 2 satisfies the requirement (1400 is earlier than the 2100 Day 2 deadline). A Day 2 duty period of 0500–2200 would not, because the 10-hour rest could not begin until 2200, after the 2100 deadline.

3. WHAT THE ANSWER IS NOT — THREE BOUNDARIES

- It is not 12 hours. The 12-hour base rest (reducible to 10 hours) in §135.273(b)(7)–(b)(8) belongs to the regime for scheduled duty periods exceeding 14 hours under the augmented-crew paragraphs, which are outside the question asked. Do not import those figures into a 14-hour-or-less duty period.
- It is not the §135.265(c) flight-crewmember reduction table (8/8/9 hours keyed to scheduled flight time) unless the operator has made the §135.273(c) election described below.
- The §135.273(b)(9) restriction — that after a 10-hour reduction the certificate holder may not schedule a flight attendant for a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest period — is triggered only by a (b)(8) 10-hour reduction. It is not triggered by the 8-hour reduction under (b)(3), though the 24-hour deadline in (b)(3) achieves a similar scheduling constraint.

4. APPLICABILITY CHECKS BEFORE THE NUMBER IS RELIED ON

- Is the person an assigned flight attendant? §135.273 applies to certificate holders that assign flight attendants to duty. §135.107 requires a flight attendant crewmember on aircraft with a passenger seating configuration, excluding any pilot seat, of more than 19. Confirm against the applicability paragraph of §135.273 and the operator's ops specs whether a particular cabin attendant is a flight attendant 'assigned to duty' within the rule; a non-crew cabin aide or passenger is outside it.
- Has the operator elected §135.273(c)? A certificate holder may instead apply the subpart F flight-crewmember flight time and duty limitations and rest requirements to flight attendants for all operations, provided it establishes written procedures that apply to all its flight attendants, incorporate the subpart F requirements as appropriate (rest facilities on board not required), add one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each excess flight crewmember, and are approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in its operations specifications. Under that election the answer changes: rest is keyed to scheduled flight time under §135.265(b) (9 consecutive hours for less than 8 hours scheduled flight time; 10 for 8 but less than 9; 11 for 9 or more), reducible under §135.265(c) to 8, 8, or 9 hours respectively, with compensatory rests of 10, 11, or 12 hours beginning no later than 24 hours after commencement of the reduced rest. If the operator has this election, the governing numbers come from its approved procedures and ops specs, not from (b)(2)–(b)(3).
- More restrictive sources. A collective bargaining agreement, the company manual/GOM, an approved fatigue risk management program, or an ops-spec limitation may impose rest longer than 9 hours or forbid the 8-hour reduction. Those sources are a floor above the regulation; they cannot lawfully authorize less than 9 hours, or less than 8 hours with the compensatory rest, for a flight attendant covered by §135.273(b).
- Exemptions/deviation. If the operator holds an exemption or deviation affecting crew rest, read it; absent one, the (b)(2)–(b)(3) scheme governs. The analysis here assumes none.
- Scheduled versus actual. The rule is written in terms of the SCHEDULED duty period and SCHEDULED rest period. The schedule must comply on its face. If actual duty runs beyond the scheduled period so that the flight attendant is actually on duty more than 14 hours, the assignment falls outside (b)(1)–(b)(3) and the operator must look to the augmented-crew paragraphs (b)(4)–(b)(7) (12 consecutive hours of rest, reducible to 10 under (b)(8), with the (b)(9) 14-hour cap on the following duty period), plus any manual provisions on revising schedules in real time.

5. DOCUMENTATION

Build the 9-hour rest (or the 8-hour rest plus the 10-hour makeup rest, with its 24-hour deadline) into the published crew schedule and pairing records, and track report and release times so that actual duty can be compared with scheduled duty. Retain duty/rest records consistent with §135.63 recordkeeping and the manual requirements applicable to the certificate holder, and record the compensatory rest explicitly whenever the 8-hour reduction is used, including the clock time the reduced rest began and the clock time the 10-hour rest is scheduled to begin, so the 24-hour test is auditable.

6. ONE-SENTENCE ANSWER

Nine consecutive hours of scheduled rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, reducible to eight consecutive hours only if a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest, with both rests falling between the end of the scheduled duty period and the start of the next duty period (§135.273(b)(2)–(b)(3)).
