# HTTP/2: current specification and its obsoleted RFCs

## Answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022, IETF Standards Track (Proposed Standard), M. Thomson and C. Benfield (Eds.) |
| 2. RFCs that RFC 9113 obsoletes | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** |

## 1. Current specification: RFC 9113

RFC 9113 is the document that currently specifies HTTP/2. Evidence from the RFC Editor's own metadata and text (fetched 2026-11-17T05:39:43Z):

- Title and date block: "RFC 9113: HTTP/2 ... June 2022. M. Thomson, Ed., C. Benfield, Ed. Proposed Standard" (rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113).
- Document header fields: "Stream: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) / RFC: 9113 / Obsoletes: 7540, 8740 / Category: Standards Track / Published: June 2022 / ISSN: 2070-1721" (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html).
- Abstract: "This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2)."

Corroboration that RFC 9113 has superseded the older document: the RFC Editor's info page for RFC 7540 carries the banner "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113." That is the obsoleted-by direction of the same chain, so the two records agree.

Currency check: as of the fetched page state (2026-11-17T05:39:43Z) the RFC 9113 info page shows no "obsoleted by" or "updated by" supersession banner, i.e. RFC 9113 was still the current HTTP/2 specification at fetch time. Because the answer is date-sensitive, the fetch timestamp is stated here so the claim can be re-verified against https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113 rather than taken on trust.

## 2. RFCs obsoleted by RFC 9113

RFC 9113 obsoletes exactly two RFCs:

1. **RFC 7540** — *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)*, May 2015, Standards Track, M. Belshe, R. Peon, M. Thomson (Ed.). This was the original HTTP/2 specification. It is now obsolete per the RFC Editor banner: "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113."
2. **RFC 8740** — *Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2*. RFC 9113 Appendix B ("Changes from RFC 7540") states: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes." RFC 8740 was a narrow update to RFC 7540's TLS requirements, so its content is folded into RFC 9113 rather than left standing as a separate update.

Primary evidence, verbatim:

- Abstract of RFC 9113: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."
- Header field: "Obsoletes: 7540, 8740".
- RFC Editor info page for RFC 7540: "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 9113. This RFC was updated, see RFC 8740."

## Terminology note (why the list has exactly two entries)

In RFC metadata, **Obsoletes** and **Updates** are distinct relations:

- *Obsoletes* means the newer document wholly replaces the older one, which should no longer be implemented or cited as current.
- *Updates* means the newer document amends specific parts of the older one while the older one remains in force.

RFC 7540 was both **updated by** RFC 8740 and **obsoleted by** RFC 9113 — these are two separate recorded facts, and only the second is what ask 2 requests. Consistently, RFC 9113's own obsoletes list contains 7540 and 8740 and nothing else; it does not list RFC 9110, RFC 9111, or RFC 9112. Those documents from the 2022 HTTP specification refactoring are related context (HTTP semantics, caching, HTTP/1.1 message syntax) but are not part of the HTTP/2 obsoletes chain, and they are deliberately excluded from the answer.

## Scope notes

- The question concerns HTTP/2 as standardized by the IETF. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) and QUIC are separate protocols and are not successors that obsolete HTTP/2; RFC 9113's obsoletes list confirms this.
- RFC 9113 does not obsolete the HTTP/1.1 message syntax; it is an alternative expression of HTTP semantics over a different framing layer.
- RFC 9113 deprecates, but does not delete, parts of RFC 7540: the priority scheme is deprecated (PRIORITY frame format and priority fields retained, semantics still described only in RFC 7540, with [HTTP-PRIORITY] recommended instead), and the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism is removed from the specification and the `HTTP2-Settings` header field registration is marked obsoleted. These are content changes inside the obsoletion, not additional obsoleted RFCs.

19th March 2026
Department for Business and Trade
Explanatory Note
(This note is not part of the Regulations)
These Regulations amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (“the 2015 Regulations”) (S.I. 2015/621). These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.
Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (regulation 4 of the 2015 Regulations).
Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
Regulation 2(3)(b) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are under the age of 18 from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(c) of the 2015 Regulations).
The apprenticeship rate applies to workers within regulation 5(1)(a) and (b) of the 2015 Regulations. Regulation 2(3)(c) of these Regulations increases the rate for such workers from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(d) of the 2015 Regulations).

A lot has changed since we gave our advice to the Government last autumn, and we are now beginning to gather evidence for recommendations later this year. The current economic uncertainty makes it essential that the Commission hears from those affected by the minimum wage and builds consensus for evidence-based recommendations.
To mark the uprating, the Low Pay Commission has published a report looking at the immediate impacts of the new rates. It has also published a consultation to inform its recommendations on future minimum wage rates.
NOTES FOR EDITORS
The LPC’s recommendations were submitted to the Government on 27 October 2025. The Government announced acceptance of those recommendations at the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 26 November.
The Government’s remit to the LPC, which determines the Commission’s work through the year, was published on 16 March and is available here.
The National Living Wage (NLW) is currently the statutory minimum wage for workers aged 21 and over. This age threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024.

verdict.summary:
HR BRIEFING NOTE — UK National Living Wage / National Minimum Wage rates effective 1 April 2026

1. THE TWO FIGURES REQUESTED

| Band | Statutory hourly rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate (to 31 March 2026) | Increase |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage — workers aged 21 and over | £12.71 | £12.21 | £0.50 (4.1%) |
| National Minimum Wage — workers aged 18 to 20 | £10.85 | £10.00 | £0.85 (8.5%) |

Both are gross hourly rates in pounds sterling. They apply from 1 April 2026 (not merely 'April 2026'); the previous rates ran to and including 31 March 2026.

2. FULL RATE TABLE FOR THE SAME UPRATING (needed because payroll cannot apply one band in isolation)

| Band | Rate from 1 April 2026 |
|---|---|
| National Living Wage, 21 and over | £12.71 |
| 18 to 20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 |
| 16 to 17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 |
| Accommodation offset (max daily deduction) | £11.10 per day |

3. LEGAL BASIS — these are enacted rates, not proposals

- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357. Made 19 March 2026; coming into force 1 April 2026; extends to England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
- Regulation 2(2): in regulation 4 of the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (the national living wage), for '£12.21' substitute '£12.71'.
- Regulation 2(3)(a): in regulation 4A(1)(b), for '£10.00' substitute '£10.85' — this is the rate for workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21.
- Regulation 2(3)(b) and (c): 16-17 rate and apprentice rate each move from £7.55 to £8.00. Regulation 2(4): accommodation offset from £10.66 to £11.10 per day.
- The Explanatory Note to the same instrument confirms in words: 'Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour… Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour.'
- Corroborated by GOV.UK's rate table (April 2026 row: £12.71 / £10.85 / £8 / £8), the Low Pay Commission report 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' (published 1 April 2026), and the LPC press release 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour' (1 April 2026).
- Provenance of the figures: LPC recommendations submitted 27 October 2025, accepted by the Government at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025, given effect by the instrument above. The statutory position is settled.

4. SCOPE AND DEFINITIONS — the four points where HR most often gets this wrong

(a) Age is the determining factor, and the NLW threshold is 21, not 23 or 25. The threshold came down from 25 to 23 in April 2021 and from 23 to 21 in April 2024. Workers aged 20 and under are on the NMW age rates, not the NLW.

(b) This is the statutory National Living Wage. It is not the 'Real Living Wage' (£12.60 / £14.05 London at the last voluntary uprating, set by the Living Wage Foundation and paid voluntarily). Do not substitute one for the other in payroll, contracts, accreditation claims or job adverts.

(c) Apprentices are the main trap. An apprentice is entitled to the Apprentice Rate (£8.00) if they are under 19, or 19 or over and in the first year of their apprenticeship. Once an apprentice is 19 or over and has completed the first year, they move to the full rate for their age — so a 21-year-old apprentice past their first year is entitled to £12.71, and a 20-year-old past their first year to £10.85. The £12.71 headline does not apply to every 21+ worker on the payroll.

(d) The rates are hourly minimums for pay reference periods. Salaried staff are not exempt: under the salaried-hours rules, pay must still be at or above the minimum for the hours actually worked. Deductions, required uniform purchases, time spent on training and travel between assignments can all push effective pay below the floor even where the headline hourly rate looks compliant. The accommodation offset is capped at £11.10 per day for April 2026 onward.

5. PAYROLL ACTIONS BEFORE THE FIRST PAY REFERENCE PERIOD BEGINNING ON OR AFTER 1 APRIL 2026

1. Extract every worker aged 21+ currently at or near £12.21 and every worker aged 18-20 at or near £10.00; these are the populations that must move on 1 April.
2. Reconcile age-band assignment against date of birth, not against job title or grade; an employee turning 21 mid-period moves bands on their birthday.
3. Re-run the apprentice check: date of birth, apprenticeship start date, and whether year one is complete.
4. Update the accommodation offset to £11.10/day for any worker in employer-provided living accommodation.
5. Check pay differentials and junior-to-standard differentials for compression — the 8.5% uplift on the 18-20 band is more than double the 4.1% on the NLW, so differentials will narrow.
6. Confirm any salary-sacrifice, deduction or charge-back arrangements do not take effective pay below the floor for the hours worked.
7. Record the rates and the SI reference in the payroll configuration log so the April 2027 uprating is applied against a clean baseline.

6. FORWARD NOTE (out of scope, but it will be asked)

Rates effective 1 April 2027 are already published on GOV.UK: £13.21 (21+), £11.27 (18-20), £8.31 (16-17 and apprentice). They are not the answer to this request and must not be applied before 1 April 2027.

7. VERIFICATION

To re-verify at any point: legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/357/made (regulations 2(2) and 2(3)(a), plus the Explanatory Note) and gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates (April 2026 row). Both must agree; if they ever diverge, the statutory instrument prevails.

Hours of Service Drivers Final Rule
FMCSA revises the hours of service (HOS) regulations to provide greater flexibility for drivers subject to those rules without adversely affecting safety. The Agency: (1) expands the short-haul exception to 150 air-miles and allows a 14-hour work shift to take place as part of the exception; (2) expands the driving window during adverse driving conditions by up to an additional 2 hours; (3) requires a 30-minute break after 8 hours of driving time (instead of on-duty time) and allows an on-duty/not driving period to qualify as the required break; and (4) modifies the sleeper berth exception to allow a driver to meet the 10-hour minimum off-duty requirement by spending at least 7, rather than at least 8 hours of that period in the berth and a minimum off-duty period of at least 2 hours spent inside or outside of the berth, provided the two periods total at least 10 hours, and that neither qualifying period counts against the 14-hour driving window.

What has changed?
Short-haul Exception
Expands the short-haul exception to 150 air-miles and allows a 14-hour work shift to take place as part of the exception.
Adverse Driving Conditions Exception
Expands the driving window during adverse driving conditions by up to an additional 2 hours.

Requires break of at least 30 consecutive minutes after 8 cumulative hours of driving time (instead of on-duty time) and allows an on-duty/not driving period to qualify as the required break.

Modifies the sleeper berth exception to allow a driver to meet the 10-hour minimum off-duty requirement by spending at least 7 hours of that period in the berth combined with a minimum off-duty period of at least 2 hours spent inside or outside the berth, provided the two periods total at least 10 hours. When used together as specified, neither qualify period counts against the 14-hour driving window.

verdict.summary:
# FMCSA Short-Haul Exception (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — Radius and Release Time

## 1. The two answers

| Ask | Answer | Unit | Regulatory basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Radius within which the driver must operate | **150** | **air miles** (172.6 statute miles) | 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(i) |
| 2. Consecutive hours within which the driver must be released from work | **14** | **consecutive hours** | 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)(ii) |

A driver qualifies for the exception from the records-of-duty-status requirement only if the driver operates **within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location** and **returns to that location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours** (plus the off-duty and carrier-recordkeeping conditions in § 4 below).

## 2. Governing text (verbatim)

49 CFR 395.1(e) — Short-haul operations:

> "(e) Short-haul operations —
> (1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
> (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
> (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
> (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
> (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
> (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing:
> (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day;
> (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day;
> (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day;
> (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

FMCSA's own summary of the same provision: *"A driver is exempt from the requirements of § 395.8 and § 395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours. Drivers using the short-haul exception in § 395.1(e)(1) must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours, and stay within a 150 air-mile radius of the work reporting location."* (FMCSA, Summary of Hours of Service Regulations; HOS Visor Card.)

## 3. How the two numbers are measured

**Radius — 150 air miles.**
- "Air mile" means the straight-line (great-circle) distance between the normal work reporting location and the driver's position — not route/road miles. The regulation supplies the conversion itself: 150 air miles = **172.6 statute miles**.
- The circle is centred on the **normal work reporting location**, i.e. the location where the driver reports to and is released from work — not the carrier's terminal, not the shipper, not the driver's residence (unless that is in fact the normal work reporting location).
- The limit is a boundary condition: the driver must remain inside it for the entire tour, not merely start and end inside it. A single excursion beyond 150 air miles defeats the exception for that tour.
- There is **no boundary-crossing allowance** attached to § 395.1(e)(1) (unlike the agricultural exception in § 395.1(k)).

**Release time — 14 consecutive hours.**
- The clock starts when the driver **comes on duty / reports for duty**, and the driver must both (a) **return to the work reporting location** and (b) be **released from work** before the 14th consecutive hour elapses.
- It is a **duty-tour clock, not a driving clock**: it runs continuously through driving, on-duty-not-driving, breaks and any off-duty time taken inside the tour. Off-duty time taken during the tour does **not** extend or pause the 14 hours.
- 14 hours is the outer bound; the exception is lost for any tour in which release occurs at or beyond the 14-hour mark.
- "Released from work" means the carrier has released the driver from duty at the normal work reporting location. A driver who returns to the location but remains on duty (e.g. continues paperwork or is held available) has not been released.
- Driver-salespersons are excluded from the release-time condition by the express carve-out in (e)(1)(ii).

## 4. Conditions precedent — all must hold for the exception to apply

1. Operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location — **ask 1**.
2. Returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours (driver-salespersons excepted) — **ask 2**.
3. Property-carrying: at least **10 consecutive hours off duty** separating each 14 hours on duty. Passenger-carrying: at least **8 consecutive hours** off duty separating each 14 hours on duty.
4. The employing motor carrier maintains and retains for **6 months** accurate and true time records of: report-for-duty time each day; total hours on duty each day; release-from-duty time each day; and, for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, total time for the preceding 7 days per § 395.8(j)(2).
5. The driver is not a driver-salesperson (for the release-time condition).

Effect when the conditions are met: the driver is exempt from § 395.8 (record of duty status) and § 395.11; FMCSA states that qualifying property and passenger carriers "are not required to use a RODS or ELD, or take a 30-minute break (§ 395.1(e)(1))." The underlying hours-of-service limits (11-hour driving, 14-hour driving window, 60/70-hour) continue to apply — the exception relieves the paperwork obligation, not the substantive driving limits.

## 5. Frequently confused neighbouring figures — none of these is the answer

| Figure | Where it comes from | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **100 air miles / 12 hours** | The pre-2020 version of § 395.1(e)(1) | **SUPERSEDED.** The 2020 HOS final rule "extends the maximum duty period allowed under the short-haul exception from 12 hours to 14 hours" and "extends the maximum radius of the short-haul exception from a 100 air-mile radius to a 150 air-mile radius." Do not use 100/12. |
| 100 air miles | § 395.1(p), motion-picture production site transportation | A different, narrow exception. Not the short-haul RODS exception. |
| 150 air miles (radius only) | § 395.1(k), agricultural commodities | Same radius figure, different exception with its own terms. |
| 14 hours / 16 hours driving cutoffs | § 395.1(e)(2), the CDL-not-required short-haul variant | See § 6 — a separate paragraph, not a substitute for the 14-hour release answer. |
| 14-hour driving window | § 395.3(a)(2) | The general HOS window; distinct from the 14-consecutive-hour report-to-release tour of (e)(1). |

## 6. Related paragraph to avoid misapplication — § 395.1(e)(2)

A second short-haul provision covers drivers of property-carrying CMVs **for which a CDL is not required** under Part 383. It uses the **same 150 air-mile radius** and requires return to the normal work reporting location **at the end of each duty tour**, but instead of a flat 14-hour release it bars driving:
- after the **14th** hour after coming on duty on **5 days** of any period of 7 consecutive days; and
- after the **16th** hour after coming on duty on **2 days** of any period of 7 consecutive days.

If a driver falls under (e)(2) rather than (e)(1), the radius answer (150 air miles) is unchanged; the release-time answer must be read from (e)(2)(iv), not from (e)(1)(ii). The question as posed — release from work within a set number of consecutive hours — is the (e)(1) formulation, so the answer given is 14.

## 7. Consequence of exceeding either limit

The exception is applied **tour by tour**. If on any day the driver exceeds the 150 air-mile radius, or is not returned and released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception does not apply for that tour and the driver must complete a record of duty status for that day (and, being then a driver required to keep RODS, must use an ELD if otherwise subject to the ELD rule). The carrier's 6-month time records under (e)(1)(iv) are what let the carrier demonstrate the exception was in fact satisfied on the days it was claimed; gaps or inaccuracies in those records undercut the claim for the affected tours.

## 8. Authorities

- 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) — short-haul operations, 150 air-mile radius driver (eCFR, current).
- 49 CFR 395.1(e)(2) — CDL-not-required short-haul variant.
- 49 CFR 395.1(k), 395.1(p) — agricultural and motion-picture exceptions (distinguishing figures).
- 49 CFR 395.3 — underlying hours-of-service limits; 395.8 — record of duty status; 395.11.
- FMCSA, *Hours of Service Drivers Final Rule* (2020 HOS revision: 150 air miles, 14-hour shift).
- FMCSA, *Summary of Hours of Service Regulations*; FMCSA *HOS Visor Card* (short-haul exception restated).

quotes.whole:
What's New
Petitions
Action
Final rule.
Summary
This final rule implements, without interpretation, the provisions of sections 815 and 828 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 ("the Act"). To conform the FAA's regulations to the self- enacting provisions in the Act, this final rule amends certain regulations to: align aircraft conditions and limitations with the term "covered aircraft" as defined in section 2307(j) of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 to increase the number of allowable passengers from 5 to 6, increase the number of occupants from 6 to 7, and increase the maximum takeoff weight from 6,000 pounds to 12,500 pounds, while excluding certain transport category rotorcraft. This final rule facilitates updates to current standards the medical form a State-licensed physician uses in completing a comprehensive medical examination. Further, this final rule amends regulations to incorporate the statutory expansion of BasicMed medical eligibility to examiners conducting practical tests or proficiency checks if they meet the requirements for operating covered aircraft under BasicMed, as provided in the Act.

quotes.whole:
3.1 What Do I Need to Fly Under BasicMed?
1. Hold a current and valid U.S. driver’s license.
2. Hold or have held a medical certificate issued by the FAA at any point after
July 14, 2006.
3. Answer the health questions on the Comprehensive Medical Examination
Checklist (CMEC).

physician complete the CMEC (be sure to keep the CMEC).
5. Take the BasicMed online medical education course. Keep the course
completion document issued to you by the course provider.
3.2 What Are My BasicMed Privileges? You can conduct any operation that you would
otherwise be able to conduct using your pilot certificate and a third-class medical
certificate, except you are limited to:
1. Fly with no more than five passengers.
2. Fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than
6,000 lbs.
3. Fly an aircraft that is authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants.
4. Flights within the United States, at an indicated airspeed of 250 knots or less,
and at an altitude at or below 18,000 feet mean sea level (MSL).
5. You may not fly for compensation or hire.

WASHINGTON – The Federal Aviation Administration updated its BasicMed regulations to allow pilots to operate larger aircraft and carry more passengers.
BasicMed, which took effect in 2017, allows pilots to fly without holding an FAA medical certificate provided they meet certain conditions.
The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required the FAA to expand BasicMed to:
Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six.
Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters.
Allow pilot examiners to conduct flight checks using BasicMed in aircraft that are covered by the BasicMed rule. Information for examiners is available here.

# BasicMed aircraft limits (United States) — current answer

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Ask | Answer | Governing condition |
|---|-----|--------|---------------------|
| 1 | Maximum takeoff weight | **12,500 lb** maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW) | Aircraft's maximum *certificated* takeoff weight must not exceed 12,500 lb |
| 2 | Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | **7 occupants** (including required flightcrew) | Aircraft must be authorized under Federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants |
| 3 | Passengers on board | **6 passengers** maximum | The flight may carry not more than 6 passengers |

These are the limits in force **on or after 12 November 2024**, which is the current state of the rule.

## 2. Regulatory basis and effective date

- **Statute:** Section 2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (PL 114-190), as amended by **Section 828 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (PL 118-63)**, which defines a "covered aircraft" and expands the BasicMed aircraft conditions.
- **Implementing rule:** Final rule, RIN 2120-AM06, Docket FAA-2024-2580, Federal Register doc. 2024-26935, published **18 November 2024**. Its own summary states it amends the regulations "to align aircraft conditions and limitations with the term 'covered aircraft' as defined in section 2307(j) of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 to increase the number of allowable passengers from 5 to 6, increase the number of occupants from 6 to 7, and increase the maximum takeoff weight from 6,000 pounds to 12,500 pounds, while excluding certain transport category rotorcraft."
- **Operative date for the aircraft limits:** **12 November 2024.** FAA Notice **N 8000.386** (dated 14 November 2024) states: "Per PL 118-63, Section 828, Expansion of BasicMed, the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024: The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, the aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and the aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board."
- **Regulatory home:** 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) (BasicMed operating conditions), read with 14 CFR part 68; for experimental aircraft the occupant cap also appears at 14 CFR 91.319(j).
- **Corroboration:** The FAA BasicMed page currently lists, under Aircraft Requirements, "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants" and "Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds," and under Operating Requirements, "Carries not more than six passengers." The FAA newsroom release of 15 November 2024 ("FAA Updates BasicMed Program") states the same three numbers.

## 3. Precision on each term

**Maximum takeoff weight (ask 1).** This is the aircraft's **maximum certificated takeoff weight** — the number in the type certificate data sheet (TCDS) or other design approval — not the actual weight of the aircraft on a given flight. An aircraft with a certificated MTOW above 12,500 lb does not qualify, even if it is flown light. Conversely, if an aircraft certificated above the ceiling is altered so that its maximum certificated takeoff weight is at or below 12,500 lb (via STC or amended TC), it can qualify; AC 68-1A §5.1.2 sets out this alteration logic for the original 6,000 lb ceiling, and the same reasoning applies to the current 12,500 lb ceiling.

**Occupants authorized (ask 2).** This is the number of occupants the **aircraft is authorized to carry under Federal law** — its design approval (TC, STC, or amended TC) — not the number of seats installed and not the number of people actually on board. AC 68-1A §5.1.2: "the aircraft's design approval would authorize the number of occupants the aircraft may carry and would contain the maximum certificated takeoff weight… So long as an aircraft's design approval (i.e., TC, STC, or ATC) authorizes the aircraft to carry no more than six occupants, that aircraft would meet the requirements." The 2017 Safety Briefing makes the practical point with the pre-expansion number: variants certificated to carry more than the ceiling do not qualify "even if they only have six seats installed." With the current ceiling, read "seven" wherever that guidance says "six." For **experimental** aircraft, which have no type certificate, the occupant cap is imposed directly by 14 CFR 91.319(j) (AC 68-1A §5.1.3 addressed the six-occupant version of that section; the 2024 final rule conformed the regulations to the new covered-aircraft definition, so confirm the amended text of § 91.319(j) before relying on it for a specific experimental aircraft).

**Passengers on board (ask 3).** This is a limit on the **flight**, not on the aircraft's paper capacity: no more than **6 passengers**. Because "occupants" includes required flightcrew, the passenger cap is what actually binds as crew size grows.

## 4. How the two occupancy numbers interact (worked cases)

Occupants = flightcrew + passengers. The aircraft may be *authorized* for up to 7; the flight may *carry* up to 6 passengers.

| Crew required/aboard | Max passengers permitted | Total occupants | Within 7-occupant authorization? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 pilot | 6 | 7 | Yes (at the limit) |
| 2 pilots | 5 | 7 | Yes (at the limit) |
| 1 pilot + 1 non-required crew/safety pilot | 5 | 7 | Yes |

A 7-occupant-authorized aircraft flown single-pilot can carry 6 passengers; the same aircraft flown with two pilots can carry 5 passengers. Both satisfy both conditions. An aircraft authorized for 8 or more occupants fails the aircraft condition regardless of how many people are aboard.

## 5. Superseded figures — do not use

The pre-12 November 2024 limits were **6,000 lb MTOW, 6 occupants authorized, 5 passengers**. These still appear in older but widely circulated documents and must not be quoted as current:

- **AC 68-1A** (3 May 2017), §3.2: "Fly with no more than five passengers… maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than 6,000 lbs… authorized to carry no more than 6 occupants."
- **FAA Safety Briefing, July/August 2017**, "The BasicMed Issue": "any aircraft with a maximum take-off weight of 6,000 pounds or less, and certified to carry not more than six occupants."
- **Notice N 8000.386** itself lists the 6,000 lb / 6 / 5 set as the conditions applicable *before* 12 November 2024, alongside the new set.

If a document you are relying on says 6,000 lb, it predates the expansion.

## 6. Verification procedure (for a specific aircraft)

1. Identify the make/model/serial number and the applicable **design approval**: TC, STC, or amended TC; for experimental, the operating limitations and 14 CFR 91.319(j).
2. Pull the **TCDS** (FAA website) or the STC/ATC paperwork and read (a) maximum certificated takeoff weight and (b) approved occupant capacity.
3. Test: MTOW ≤ 12,500 lb **and** authorized occupants ≤ 7 **and** aircraft is not a transport category rotorcraft excluded from the expansion.
4. At dispatch, test: passengers aboard ≤ 6 and total occupants ≤ 7.
5. Record the basis (TCDS revision date / STC number) in the flight or training records.

## 7. Caveats

- **Transport category rotorcraft.** The 2024 expansion excludes certain transport category rotorcraft. For a transport category helicopter, do not assume the 12,500 lb / 7-occupant figures apply; verify against the amended rule text and the covered-aircraft definition before flight.
- **Other BasicMed conditions are unchanged and not part of this answer.** BasicMed flight operations remain limited to VFR or IFR, within the United States (or another country in which BasicMed is authorized), at or below 18,000 ft MSL, at an indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots, and not for compensation or hire. The whole flight must comply — a BasicMed pilot cannot act as PIC for any portion of a flight that exceeds these limits, even if another pilot aboard holds a medical certificate.
- **Pilot-side eligibility is separate.** Holding a valid U.S. driver's license, having held an FAA medical certificate at any point after 14 July 2006, a current CMEC from a state-licensed physician, and a completed BasicMed online course are prerequisites independent of the three aircraft numbers above.
- **Currency of this answer.** Figures are as of the sources fetched 17 November 2026, reflecting the rule effective 18 November 2024 and the 12 November 2024 statutory trigger. Any later rulemaking or new FAA guidance would supersede them; re-check 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) and the FAA BasicMed page before relying on this in a checkride, insurance, or enforcement context.

Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 395 appear at 66 FR 49874, Oct. 1, 2001.






§ 395.5 Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.


Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1:




(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:




(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or






(2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.








(b) No motor carrier shall permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle to drive, nor shall any driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, for any period after—




(1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or





(2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.

verdict.summary:
# Hours of service for the driver of a passenger-carrying CMV (motorcoach) — US federal rules

**Governing provision:** 49 CFR 395.5, *Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles* (49 CFR Part 395, Subpart A), read '[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1.' Quoted text below is from the current eCFR text of § 395.5 and the 2025 printed CFR (Title 49, Vol. 5), both fetched for this task.

## 0. Applicability check (do this first — everything below depends on it)

Part 395 splits into two parallel rule sets: § 395.3 for **property**-carrying CMVs and § 395.5 for **passenger**-carrying CMVs. The limits are not interchangeable, so confirm the vehicle is passenger-carrying before applying any number here.

A motorcoach is a passenger-carrying CMV: 49 CFR 390.5 defines a CMV as a self-propelled or towed motor vehicle used on a highway in interstate commerce to transport passengers or property when the vehicle, among other tests, '(2) Is designed or used to transport more than 8 passengers (including the driver) for compensation' or has a GVWR/GCWR of 10,001 lb or more. A motorcoach carrying passengers for compensation meets that test. If the operation is instead a property-carrying CMV (e.g., a courier van, or a bus converted to freight), § 395.3 applies and the numbers are 11 / 10 / 14 — **not** the numbers below.

## 1. The three limits (the answers)

### Ask 1 — Maximum driving: **10 hours**
§ 395.5(a)(1): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV '[m]ore than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.'

That is 10 hours of *driving time* accumulated in the on-duty period that begins at the end of the 8 consecutive hours off duty. It is not 10 hours of on-duty time, and it is not extendable by on-duty non-driving work.

### Ask 2 — Required consecutive off duty: **8 hours**
Same subsection: the 10-hour driving allowance is measured 'following 8 consecutive hours off duty.' The 8 hours must be **consecutive** and must be **off duty** (not on duty, not driving). This is the sharpest difference from the property-carrying rule, which requires 10 consecutive hours off duty (§ 395.3(a)(1)). A motorcoach driver does **not** need 10 consecutive hours under the federal passenger rule.

Note on sleeper berths: under § 395.2, sleeper-berth time is not 'on-duty time' (on-duty time excludes sleeper-berth periods), so sleeper-berth time counts toward the 8 consecutive hours off duty for a passenger-carrying driver. Unlike the property rule, § 395.5 contains **no** split sleeper-berth provision and § 395.1(g)'s sleeper-berth pairing rules are written for property-carrying drivers — do not try to run a 7/3 or 8/2 split against the passenger 8-hour requirement. (Confidence: high on the text; the sleeper-berth-counts-as-off-duty point is settled practice, but confirm with counsel if it is load-bearing for a specific schedule.)

### Ask 3 — On-duty ceiling for driving: **15 hours**
§ 395.5(a)(2): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, 'for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.'

Driving is prohibited once the driver has been on duty 15 hours measured from the end of the last 8 consecutive hours off duty. The 15-hour clock is an **on-duty** clock, not a driving clock: all on-duty non-driving time (pre-trip inspection, loading, waiting at the terminal, dispatch, paperwork) counts against it. The 15-hour window and the 10-hour driving allowance run concurrently — the driver's 10 driving hours must be completed inside the same 15-hour on-duty window.

## 2. Cumulative weekly limits (a second, independent driving prohibition)

§ 395.5(b) bars driving 'for any period after—'
- **(b)(1)** '[h]aving been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week'; or
- **(b)(2)** '[h]aving been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.'

These are rolling multi-day totals, not a daily figure, so they are reported here rather than as the answer to ask 3. Which one applies is a property of the **carrier's operating schedule**, not the driver's preference: a carrier that runs CMVs every day of the week is on the 70/8 cycle; one that does not is on the 60/7 cycle. A driver used by more than one carrier must count on-duty time for all of them (§ 395.5(b): 'regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services').

Practical effect: a driver may be well inside the 10-hour and 15-hour limits and still be prohibited from driving because the 60- or 70-hour total is exhausted. Conversely, hitting 60/70 bars **driving**; it does not by its terms bar remaining on duty on non-driving tasks, though the time still accrues to the cycle.

**No 34-hour restart.** The § 395.3(c) restart is a property-carrying provision. § 395.5 has no restart paragraph. A passenger-carrying driver regains driving eligibility only when enough off-duty time has passed that the prior on-duty hours roll out of the 7- or 8-day window.

## 3. What does not apply (importing these would give wrong numbers)

| Rule | Applies to | Status for passenger-carrying |
|---|---|---|
| 11-hour driving limit, § 395.3(a)(1) | Property | Does not apply — use 10 (§ 395.5(a)(1)) |
| 14-hour driving window, § 395.3(a)(2) | Property | Does not apply — use the 15-hour **on-duty** limit (§ 395.5(a)(2)) |
| 10 consecutive hours off duty, § 395.3(a)(1) | Property | Does not apply — 8 consecutive hours (§ 395.5(a)(1)) |
| 34-hour restart, § 395.3(c) | Property | Does not apply |
| Split sleeper berth, § 395.1(g) | Property | Does not apply — take the 8 hours in one block |
| Short-haul exemption, § 395.1(e) | Property (CDL and non-CDL) | Does not apply to passenger-carrying operations |

## 4. Exceptions that could move the numbers — flag, don't silently apply

- **Adverse driving conditions, § 395.1(b)(1).** A driver who encounters adverse driving conditions (as defined in § 395.2) 'may drive and be permitted or required to drive a commercial motor vehicle for the period of time needed to complete the run.' This relieves the **driving-time** limit. Because § 395.5(a)(2) is an **on-duty** limit, the exception should not be read to extend the 15-hour on-duty prohibition — driving after the 15th on-duty hour remains a violation. Treat this as the conservative reading and confirm before relying on any extension of the 15-hour clock. (Confidence: moderate-high; this is an interpretation point, not quoted text.)
- **State law.** Part 395 governs CMVs in **interstate** commerce. A state may impose stricter hours-of-service requirements, and purely **intrastate** motorcoach operations are governed by the state's own HOS rules (which must be compatible with the federal rules under the MCSAP framework, 49 CFR Part 350). If the operation never crosses a state line, verify the state rule before using these numbers.
- **Statutory/regulatory exemptions, § 395.1 generally.** § 395.5 is expressly '[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1.' If any exemption (e.g., a specific statutory exemption for a particular operation) is claimed, the numbers above are displaced to that extent.
- **Company policy.** Carrier policy may be stricter than the legal minimum; it cannot be looser.

## 5. Worked example (checking the arithmetic against all three limits)

Driver comes off 8 consecutive hours off duty at 06:00. On duty at 06:00.

- 15-hour on-duty ceiling: 06:00 + 15 h = **21:00**. No driving at or after 21:00.
- 10-hour driving allowance: at most **10:00** of the 15 hours may be driving; the other 5 hours (or more) must be on-duty non-driving or off duty.
- Suppose the driver drives 4 h, is on duty non-driving 1 h, drives 4 h, takes 1 h off duty, drives 2 h → 10 h driving reached at 18:00, 12 h on duty. Driving is over: the 10-hour limit is exhausted at 18:00 even though the 15-hour window runs to 21:00. Additional on-duty non-driving work may continue to 21:00, but not driving.
- Suppose instead the driver's driving is light: 6 h driving but 15 h on duty (long loading/waiting). Driving stops at 21:00 regardless of the 4 unused driving hours.
- Separately test the cycle: if the carrier runs CMVs every day and the driver already has 68 on-duty hours in the last 8 days, the driver may add at most 2 more on-duty hours before the § 395.5(b)(2) driving prohibition attaches, regardless of the daily clocks.

## 6. Recordkeeping context

Compliance with all three limits is evidenced by the driver's record of duty status under § 395.8 (24-hour duty-status grid, with the ELD requirements of Part 395 Subpart B for drivers subject to the ELD rule). Carriers must retain records of duty status and supporting documents for at least 6 months (§ 395.8(k)(1)). When a driver is used by more than one carrier, the driver must furnish each carrier a copy of the record of duty status covering all duty time in the 24-hour period, and a carrier using a driver for the first time or intermittently must obtain a signed statement of the driver's total on-duty time for the preceding 7 days and the time last relieved from duty (§ 395.8(j)). Those statements are how the 60/70-hour total is verified across carriers.

## 7. Verification of every stated number against every stated threshold

| Stated value | Source | Cross-check |
|---|---|---|
| 10 h driving | § 395.5(a)(1) | 10 ≤ 15 (on-duty ceiling) — consistent; driving cannot outlast the window |
| 8 h consecutive off duty | § 395.5(a)(1) | 8 < 10 (property rule) — correct direction for passenger; 8 h resets both the 10-h and 15-h clocks, so no residual clock conflicts |
| 15 h on duty | § 395.5(a)(2) | Measured from end of the same 8 consecutive hours off duty as the 10-h limit — single shared anchor, no dual-anchor inconsistency |
| 60 h / 7 days | § 395.5(b)(1) | Applies only when carrier does not operate CMVs every day; mutually exclusive with (b)(2) |
| 70 h / 8 days | § 395.5(b)(2) | Applies only when carrier operates CMVs every day; mutually exclusive with (b)(1) |
| No 34-h restart | § 395.5 text contains no restart; § 395.3(c) is property-only | Does not create a fourth number that could contradict the three answers |

No stated value exceeds or contradicts another stated limit.

## 8. One-line answer for the driver

**Drive no more than 10 hours, after at least 8 consecutive hours off duty, and never after you have been on duty 15 hours — and in any case never after 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day) or 70 hours on duty in 8 consecutive days (carrier operating every day).**

verdict.summary:
# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR Part 135

## 1. Answer

| Item | Value | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum rest after a scheduled duty period of **14 hours or less** | **9 consecutive hours** (scheduled rest period) | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(2) |
| Lowest rest to which that may be reduced | **8 consecutive hours** | 14 CFR 135.273(b)(3) |

Both figures are *consecutive* hours. There is no authority in 135.273 to go below 8 consecutive hours for this duty-period band.

## 2. Governing text (verbatim, 14 CFR 135.273, current e-CFR / 2026 CFR edition)

**135.273(a) — definitions:**

> **Duty period** means the period of elapsed time between reporting for an assignment involving flight time and release from that assignment by the certificate holder. The time is calculated using either Coordinated Universal Time or local time to reflect the total elapsed time.
>
> **Flight attendant** means an individual, other than a flight crewmember, who is assigned by the certificate holder, in accordance with the required minimum crew complement under the certificate holder's operations specifications or in addition to that minimum complement, to duty in an aircraft during flight time and whose duties include but are not necessarily limited to cabin-safety-related responsibilities.
>
> **Rest period** means the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise.

**135.273(b) — duty period limitations and rest requirements:**

> (b) Except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section, a certificate holder may assign a duty period to a flight attendant only when the applicable duty period limitations and rest requirements of this paragraph are met.
>
> (1) Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours.
>
> (2) Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
>
> (3) The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

**135.273(b)(10), (11) — absolute bars:**

> (10) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section.
>
> (11) No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period.

**135.261(e) — scope (why an on-demand charter holder is covered):**

> (e) Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part.

Note the contrast with 135.261(b)–(d): the flight crewmember sections (135.265/267/269) apply selectively by operation type, but 135.273 applies to **all** Part 135 operations. No election, ops-spec amendment, or scheduled-service finding is needed to make the flight attendant rule apply.

## 3. The five conditions on the reduction to 8 hours

A reduction from 9 to 8 consecutive hours is lawful only if **all** of the following are satisfied:

1. **Floor.** The rest is not less than 8 consecutive hours. (b)(3)
2. **Compensatory rest.** The flight attendant is given a *subsequent* rest period of **at least 10 consecutive hours**. (b)(3)
3. **Clock deadline measured from the START of the reduced rest.** That subsequent rest must be *scheduled to begin* no later than **24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** — not 24 hours after its end, and not 24 hours after the duty period ended. (b)(3)
4. **Placement.** Both the reduced rest and the subsequent rest must fall between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. (b)(2), (b)(3)
5. **No work during rest.** No duty of any kind may be assigned during either rest period; a rest period is "free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise" — no standby/reserve availability, no call-in, no administrative or training duty. (b)(11), (a)

Failure of condition 2, 3, or 4 means the rest was not reducible: the flight attendant was entitled to the full 9 consecutive hours, and assigning duty off an 8-hour rest is a violation of (b)(2) and (b)(10).

## 4. Worked timeline (verification of the arithmetic)

Scheduled duty period 06:00–20:00 local, 14.0 hours (at the top of the "14 hours or less" band).

**Baseline (no reduction):** rest begins at release, 20:00. 9 consecutive hours → duty may not be assigned before **05:00** the next day.

**Reduced:** rest begins 20:00, 8 consecutive hours → earliest assignment **04:00** the next day. Because reduced rest began at 20:00, the compensatory 10-hour rest must **begin no later than 20:00 the following day**. Example that complies: next duty period 04:00–14:00 (10.0 hours), release 14:00, subsequent rest 14:00→00:00 = 10.0 consecutive hours, which begins 14:00, i.e., 18 hours after the 20:00 start of the reduced rest (≤ 24). Complies.

Example that fails: next duty 04:00–22:00, release 22:00. Subsequent rest would begin 22:00, which is 26 hours after the 20:00 start of the reduced rest — outside the 24-hour window. The 8-hour reduction was therefore not available; the crewmember needed 9 hours and could not be assigned at 04:00.

## 5. Point that is most often gotten wrong

**135.273(b)(9) does not apply to this reduction.** That paragraph reads:

> (9) Notwithstanding paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, if a certificate holder elects to reduce the rest period to 10 hours as authorized by paragraph (b)(8) of this section, the certificate holder may not schedule a flight attendant for a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest period.

By its terms it is triggered only by a **10-hour** reduction under **(b)(8)**, which is the rest attaching to *extended* duty periods of more than 14 (up to 20) hours under (b)(4)–(b)(6). It imposes no 14-hour next-duty cap on an 8-hour reduction under (b)(3). Do not import it; doing so would ground aircraft unnecessarily. Conversely, do not import the (b)(3) 10-hour compensatory-rest condition into a (b)(8) 10-hour reduction — (b)(8) requires 14 consecutive hours of subsequent rest.

## 6. Context: the longer-duty branches (for completeness, not part of the answer)

- (b)(4): scheduled duty >14 but ≤16 hours, permitted if at least **one** additional flight attendant beyond the ops-spec minimum is assigned.
- (b)(5): >16 but ≤18 hours, at least **two** additional flight attendants.
- (b)(6): >18 but ≤20 hours, at least **three** additional flight attendants, and the duty period must include one or more flights landing or taking off outside the 48 contiguous states and D.C.
- (b)(7): a flight attendant scheduled to >14 but ≤20 hours must get **12 consecutive hours** of scheduled rest.
- (b)(8): that 12 hours may be scheduled or reduced to **10 consecutive hours** if followed by at least **14 consecutive hours** of subsequent rest beginning no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest; and (b)(9) then caps the next duty period at 14 hours in the following 24.

Summary of the bands: ≤14 h duty → 9 h rest, reducible to 8 h (10 h makeup). >14–20 h duty → 12 h rest, reducible to 10 h (14 h makeup, plus the 14-hour next-duty cap).

## 7. Two caveats the operator must clear before applying the 9/8 answer

**(a) 135.273(c) alternative election.** A certificate holder may, instead of (b), apply the *flight crewmember* flight time/duty/rest rules to its flight attendants, provided it establishes written procedures that apply to all flight attendants in its operation, incorporate the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate (on-board rest facilities not required), add one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each flight crewmember above the type-certificate minimum, and are **approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the certificate holder's operations specifications**. If — and only if — this operator holds such approved procedures, the answer is not 9/8 but the flight-crewmember table of 135.265(b)/(c): 9 hours for <8 h scheduled flight time, 10 hours for 8 to <9 h, 11 hours for ≥9 h, reducible respectively to 8, 8, and 9 hours with compensating 10/11/12-hour rest beginning within 24 hours of the start of the reduced rest. **Action: pull the ops specs and confirm no 135.273(c) election is in effect.** Absent that, 9/8 governs.

**(b) Whether a flight attendant is assigned at all.** 135.273 governs only individuals meeting the (a) definition — assigned per the ops-spec minimum crew complement or in addition to it, with cabin-safety duties. If a given flight is not required to and does not carry a flight attendant, the rule has no subject. The question presumes one is assigned; if the operator's seating configuration/ops specs never require one, say so rather than applying 9/8 to a crewmember who is not a "flight attendant."

Neither caveat makes the question unanswerable — the Part 135 flight attendant rule is 9 → 8 — but both change the number if present, so they belong in the compliance file.

## 8. Assumptions and limits of this answer

- Source is the current e-CFR text of 135.273 and the 2026 CFR (GovInfo) edition of Part 135, retrieved 2026-11-17. The section has been stable since the 1994 amendments (Amdt. 135-52); still, re-verify against e-CFR at the time of any enforcement-sensitive use, and check for any FAA-issued exemption, letter of interpretation, or ops-spec deviation held by this specific certificate holder.
- This is the **regulatory floor**. A collective bargaining agreement or company manual may impose more rest; the more restrictive term controls as a matter of contract/policy, not regulation.
- The rest table is keyed to the **scheduled** duty period. The regulation contains no separate rest table keyed to an actual duty period that overruns its schedule. Where actual duty exceeds the schedule, the rest is still computed from actual release (a rest period cannot begin before release, since the crewmember is not yet free of responsibility), but whether an overrun past 14 hours pulls the flight into the (b)(4)–(b)(7) regime is a question of how the assignment was scheduled and is not resolved by the text alone — treat an overrun past 14 hours conservatively (12 hours of rest) and obtain FSDO/legal confirmation. This is the one point in the answer that is interpretive rather than textual.
- Time basis: the holder must use either UTC or local time consistently to reflect total elapsed time (135.273(a), "Duty period"). Document which basis the schedule uses.

## 9. Compliance checklist for the scheduling/dispatch system

1. Compute scheduled duty period length (report to release).
2. If ≤14.0 h → required rest = 9 consecutive hours, measured from actual release.
3. To use 8 hours, flag the pairing and verify in the system: (i) 8 ≥ rest ≥ 8; (ii) a subsequent rest block ≥10 consecutive hours exists; (iii) that block begins ≤ (start of reduced rest + 24:00); (iv) both blocks lie between end of the scheduled duty period and start of the subsequent duty period.
4. Hard-block any assignment during a required rest period (b)(11); do not allow reserve/standby or administrative duty to be coded into a rest block.
5. If any condition in step 3 fails, restore the rest to 9 hours and re-solve the pairing.
6. Confirm the ops specs contain no 135.273(c) election before deploying the 9/8 logic as the rule engine's default.

quotes.whole:
Appendix B. Changes from RFC 7540
This revision includes the following substantive changes:
Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes.
The priority scheme defined in RFC 7540 is deprecated. Definitions for the format of the PRIORITY frame and the priority fields in the HEADERS frame have been retained, plus the rules governing when PRIORITY frames can be sent and received, but the semantics of these fields are only described in RFC 7540. The priority signaling scheme from RFC 7540 was not successful. Using the simpler signaling in [HTTP-PRIORITY] is recommended.
The HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism is deprecated and no longer specified in this document. It was never widely deployed, with plaintext HTTP/2 users choosing to use the prior-knowledge implementation instead.
Validation for field names and values has been narrowed. The validation that is mandatory for intermediaries is precisely defined, and error reporting for requests has been amended to encourage sending 400-series status codes.
The ranges of codepoints for settings and frame types that were reserved for Experimental Use are now available for general use.

Appendix B. Changes from RFC 7540
This revision includes the following substantive changes:
Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes.
The priority scheme defined in RFC 7540 is deprecated. Definitions for the format of the PRIORITY frame and the priority fields in the HEADERS frame have been retained, plus the rules governing when PRIORITY frames can be sent and received, but the semantics of these fields are only described in RFC 7540. The priority signaling scheme from RFC 7540 was not successful. Using the simpler signaling in [HTTP-PRIORITY] is recommended.
The HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism is deprecated and no longer specified in this document. It was never widely deployed, with plaintext HTTP/2 users choosing to use the prior-knowledge implementation instead.
Validation for field names and values has been narrowed. The validation that is mandatory for intermediaries is precisely defined, and error reporting for requests has been amended to encourage sending 400-series status codes.
The ranges of codepoints for settings and frame types that were reserved for Experimental Use are now available for general use.

2.1.  Document Organization
The HTTP/2 specification is split into four parts:
o  Starting HTTP/2 (Section 3) covers how an HTTP/2 connection is
initiated.
o  The frame (Section 4) and stream (Section 5) layers describe the
way HTTP/2 frames are structured and formed into multiplexed
streams.
o  Frame (Section 6) and error (Section 7) definitions include
details of the frame and error types used in HTTP/2.
o  HTTP mappings (Section 8) and additional requirements (Section 9)
describe how HTTP semantics are expressed using frames and
streams.
While some of the frame and stream layer concepts are isolated from
HTTP, this specification does not define a completely generic frame
layer.  The frame and stream layers are tailored to the needs of the
HTTP protocol and server push.

# HTTP/2: current specification and what it obsoletes

## Answer

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, June 2022, Standards Track (Proposed Standard), IETF HTTPBIS working group; editors M. Thomson and C. Benfield |
| 2 | RFCs that RFC 9113 obsoletes | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** (exactly two) |

Source of record: RFC Editor subject page for HTTP/2 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/), RFC Editor info page for RFC 9113 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113), IETF Datatracker doc pages for RFC 9113 (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/) and RFC 7540 (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7540/), and the HTTPWG published copy of the RFC (https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html). All fetched 2026-11-17T05:46:51Z.

---

## 1. The current specification: RFC 9113

RFC 9113, *HTTP/2*, was published June 2022 on the IETF Standards Track as a Proposed Standard. It is the document the RFC Editor files under the HTTP/2 subject area as the current entry, and the same page marks its two predecessors as obsoleted by it.

Evidence, quoted from the fetched pages:

- RFC 9113 header block (httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html): `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740`, `Category: Standards Track`, `June 2022`, title `HTTP/2`.
- RFC 9113 abstract: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."
- RFC Editor HTTP/2 subject page, newest-first: "RFC 9113: HTTP/2 — Proposed Standard — M. Thomson, C. Benfield — June 2022 — IETF publication".
- Same page, RFC 7540 entry: "Obsoleted by RFC 9113". Same page, RFC 8740 entry: "Obsoleted by RFC 9113".
- Datatracker rfc9113 page repeats the abstract sentence verbatim.

Two clarifications a reader will otherwise get wrong:

- **It is a Proposed Standard, not an Internet Standard.** RFC 9113's Status of This Memo reads "This is an Internet Standards Track document." That is a track, not a maturity level of Internet Standard. Do not describe HTTP/2 as an Internet Standard.
- **httpwg.org/specs/rfc9113.html is the same document, not a competing spec.** It is the HTTP Working Group's HTML rendering of RFC 9113. Cite it as a rendering of RFC 9113, never as an alternative to it.

---

## 2. What RFC 9113 obsoletes: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740

The authoritative field is the `Obsoletes` header, which names two documents:

| Obsoleted RFC | Title | Publication | Authors | Why it is in the list |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RFC 7540** | *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)* | May 2015, Proposed Standard | M. Belshe, R. Peon, M. Thomson (ed.) | It was the original HTTP/2 specification; RFC 9113 is its full revision. |
| **RFC 8740** | *Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2* | February 2020, Proposed Standard | D. Benjamin | It was a stand-alone addendum to RFC 7540; RFC 9113 folds TLS 1.3 usage into the main text, so the addendum is absorbed rather than left dangling. |

RFC 9113's own Appendix B states this directly: "Use of TLS 1.3 was defined based on [RFC8740], which this document obsoletes."

**The obsoleted set is exactly {RFC 7540, RFC 8740}. Answering "RFC 7540" alone is incomplete and is the most common error on this question.**

---

## 3. Obsoletes vs Updates — the distinction that must not be collapsed

These are different relations and RFC 9113's header uses only the first for these two documents:

```
RFC 7540  (HTTP/2, 2015) ──obsoleted by──► RFC 9113
RFC 8740  (TLS 1.3 w/ HTTP/2, 2020) ──obsoleted by──► RFC 9113
         └── RFC 8740 itself "updates RFC 7540" (an earlier, separate edge)
```

- RFC 8740's abstract, per the RFC Editor subject page: "This document updates RFC 7540 by forbidding TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication..." — so 8740 was an *Updates* document in 2020, and became an *Obsoleted* document in 2022. Both statements are true of different time periods; neither contradicts the other.
- RFC 9113's captured header shows an `Obsoletes` field and no `Updates` field. That is an observation about the fetched header block; if the Updates relation matters for a downstream registry, confirm against https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113 rather than inferring from this memo.

---

## 4. What RFC 9113 does NOT obsolete (guard against over-listing)

The following RFCs appear on the RFC Editor HTTP/2 subject page with no "Obsoleted by" marker and remain in force. They must not be added to the answer to ask 2:

| RFC | Title | Relation to RFC 9113 |
|---|---|---|
| RFC 7541 | HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2 | Still current; RFC 9113 references it for field compression. Not obsoleted. |
| RFC 8441 | Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2 | Still current. Not obsoleted. |
| RFC 8336 | The ORIGIN HTTP/2 Frame | Still current. Not obsoleted. |

Context only, not part of either answer: RFC 9218 (*Extensible Prioritization Scheme for HTTP*) is *recommended* by RFC 9113 §5.3.2 and Appendix B in place of the deprecated RFC 7540 priority scheme; RFC 9113 does not obsolete it, and the RFC 7540 priority *signalling semantics* are deprecated but the frame/field formats are retained for interoperability.

---

## 5. Reproducible verification procedure

Anyone re-checking this should run the following and expect the stated result. It takes about two minutes.

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/subjects/http2/ with sort = "Newest first".
   - Expect the first entry to be RFC 9113, June 2022, Proposed Standard.
   - Expect the RFC 7540 and RFC 8740 entries each to carry the badge "Obsoleted by RFC 9113".
   - Expect no other entry on the page to carry an "Obsoleted by RFC 9113" badge.
2. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113 and read the header block.
   - Expect `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740` — two values, comma-separated.
   - Expect `Category: Standards Track` and a June 2022 date.
3. Open https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ and read the abstract.
   - Expect the sentence "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."
4. Cross-check the reverse direction on https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7540/.
   - Expect the 2015 document to be flagged as obsoleted by RFC 9113, confirming the edge is recorded on both ends.
5. Record the lookup date with the answer. RFC status is time-varying; an answer without a lookup date is not verifiable later.

Consistency check on the final answer: the obsoleted list must contain exactly the two identifiers in the `Obsoletes` header, no more and no fewer. If a lookup returns anything other than {7540, 8740}, the header and the subject page disagree and the header wins.

---

## 6. Assumptions made (stated, not hidden)

1. **"Current" = the most recently published IETF Standards Track RFC for HTTP/2 as of the lookup date 2026-11-17.** It does not mean "the version a particular product implements," and it does not mean a working-copy draft.
2. **Internet-Drafts are excluded.** A draft that may eventually supersede RFC 9113 does not make RFC 9113 non-current; only publication of a successor RFC does.
3. **Errata are excluded from the answer.** Errata correct text within RFC 9113; they do not change its number and do not obsolete it. Consult https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/ for the errata list if the corrected text matters.
4. **The obsoleted list is taken from the `Obsoletes` header**, i.e. the direct predecessors named by RFC 9113, not a transitive closure over the whole historical HTTP/2 document lineage.
5. **RFC 9113 has not been superseded as of 2026-11-17** per the fetched RFC Editor and Datatracker records. If this memo is reused later, re-run §5 first.

The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 No. 357 xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom"

TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT

The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026


Made

The Secretary of State makes these Regulations in exercise of the powers conferred by sections 1(3), 2(1), (2)(d) and (5), 3(2)(b) and 51(1)(a) of the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 (“the 1998 Act”)(1).

A draft of these Regulations was laid before Parliament in accordance with section 51(5) of the 1998 Act and approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament.



Citation, commencement and extent

1.—(1) These Regulations may be cited as the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026.

(2) These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.

(3) These Regulations extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

Amendments to the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015

2.—(1) The National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015(2) are amended as follows.

(2) In regulation 4 (the national living wage) for “£12.21” substitute “£12.71”.

(3) In regulation 4A(1) (workers who qualify for the national minimum wage at a different rate)—

(a)in sub-paragraph (b) for “£10.00” substitute “£10.85”;

(b)in sub-paragraph (c) for “£7.55” substitute “£8.00”;

(c)in sub-paragraph (d) for “£7.55” substitute “£8.00”.

(4) In regulation 16(1) (amount for provision of living accommodation) for “£10.66” substitute “£11.10”.




Name

Title

Department for Business and Trade

DATE




Explanatory Note

(This note is not part of the Regulations)
 
These Regulations amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (“the 2015 Regulations”) (S.I. 2015/621). These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026.
  
Regulation 2(2) increases the rate of the national living wage for workers who are aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour (regulation 4 of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are aged 18 or over (but not yet aged 21) from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(3)(b) increases the rate of the national minimum wage for workers who are under the age of 18 from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(c) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
The apprenticeship rate applies to workers within regulation 5(1)(a) and (b) of the 2015 Regulations. Regulation 2(3)(c) of these Regulations increases the rate for such workers from £7.55 to £8.00 per hour (regulation 4A(1)(d) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
Regulation 2(4) increases the accommodation offset amount which is applicable where any employer provides a worker with living accommodation from £10.66 to £11.10 for each day that accommodation is provided (regulation 16(1) of the 2015 Regulations).
  
A full regulatory impact assessment of the effect that this instrument will have on the costs of business and the voluntary sector is available from the Employment Rights Directorate, Department for Business and Trade, Old Admiralty Building, London SW1A 2AY and is annexed to the Explanatory Memorandum which is available alongside the instrument on www.legislation.gov.uk.

A lot has changed since we gave our advice to the Government last autumn, and we are now beginning to gather evidence for recommendations later this year. The current economic uncertainty makes it essential that the Commission hears from those affected by the minimum wage and builds consensus for evidence-based recommendations.
To mark the uprating, the Low Pay Commission has published a report looking at the immediate impacts of the new rates. It has also published a consultation to inform its recommendations on future minimum wage rates.

quotes.whole:
National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage
The National Minimum Wage (NMW) and National Living Wage (NLW) are a minimum amount per hour that most workers in the UK are entitled to be paid.
The minimum wage legislation was established in the National Minimum Wage Act 1998. The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage are defined on 1 April every year, based on this legislation.
There are different rates of minimum wage depending on a worker's age and whether they are an apprentice. In April 2026, the NLW applied to employees aged 21 years and over, and the NMW applied to employees aged between 16 and 20 years.
The government's NLW was introduced on 1 April 2016 and applied to employees aged 25 years and over. The maximum age for the NLW has changed over the years. From 2024 onwards, it applies to employees aged 21 years and over.
On the ASHE reference date in April 2026, the NMW and NLW rates were:
£12.71 for employees aged 21 years and over
£10.85 for employees aged 18 to 20 years
£8 for employees aged 16 to 17 years
£8 for apprentices aged 16 to 18 years and those aged 19 years or over who are in the first year of their apprenticeship

verdict.summary:
UK STATUTORY MINIMUM WAGE RATES EFFECTIVE 1 APRIL 2026

ANSWERS
1. National Living Wage (workers aged 21 and over): £12.71 per hour.
2. National Minimum Wage, 18-20 Year Old Rate (workers aged 18, 19 or 20): £10.85 per hour.

Both are in pounds sterling, per hour, at the officially published precision (nearest penny). Both took effect on 1 April 2026 and apply UK-wide (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland) — the instrument extends to all four nations and there is no regional or sector variation in the statutory rate.

LEGAL BASIS
The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/357), made under ss.1(3), 2(1), (2)(d) and (5), 3(2)(b) and 51(1)(a) of the National Minimum Wage Act 1998, laid in draft under s.51(5) and approved by resolution of each House, coming into force 1 April 2026. They amend the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (S.I. 2015/621):
- reg. 2(2): reg. 4 (the national living wage) — '£12.21' replaced by '£12.71'.
- reg. 2(3)(a): reg. 4A(1)(b) (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21) — '£10.00' replaced by '£10.85'.
- reg. 2(3)(b): reg. 4A(1)(c) (under 18) — '£7.55' replaced by '£8.00'.
- reg. 2(3)(c): reg. 4A(1)(d) (apprentice rate) — '£7.55' replaced by '£8.00'.
- reg. 2(4): reg. 16(1) (accommodation offset) — '£10.66' replaced by '£11.10' per day.

CORROBORATION
- Low Pay Commission, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026': table of rates to apply from 1 April 2026 — NLW (21 and over) £12.71 (+£0.50, 4.1%); 18-20 Year Old Rate £10.85 (+£0.85, 8.5%); 16-17 Year Old Rate £8.00 (+£0.45, 6.0%); Apprentice Rate £8.00 (+£0.45, 6.0%); Accommodation Offset £11.10 (+£0.44, 4.1%).
- Low Pay Commission press release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour', published 1 April 2026: rates 'came into force from 1 April 2026'. Notes the LPC's recommendations were submitted 27 October 2025 and accepted in full by the Government at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025.
- GOV.UK 'National Minimum Wage rates' page: April 2026 row — 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; under 18 £8; apprentice £8. The same page also carries an April 2027 row (£13.21 / £11.27 / £8.31 / £8.31), which is a forward rate and is NOT the answer to either question.
- ONS, 'Low and high pay in the UK: 2026' (ASHE): 'On the ASHE reference date in April 2026, the NMW and NLW rates were: £12.71 for employees aged 21 years and over; £10.85 for employees aged 18 to 20 years; £8 for employees aged 16 to 17 years; £8 for apprentices...'.

ARITHMETIC CHECK
12.21 + 0.50 = 12.71; 0.50 / 12.21 = 4.09% (published 4.1%).
10.00 + 0.85 = 10.85; 0.85 / 10.00 = 8.5% (published 8.5%).
10.85 / 12.71 = 85.4%, consistent with the 18-20 rate as a proportion of the adult rate.
Accommodation offset: 10.66 + 0.44 = 11.10; 0.44 / 10.66 = 4.13% (published 4.1%).
16-17 and apprentice: 7.55 + 0.45 = 8.00; 0.45 / 7.55 = 5.96% (published 6.0%).
All stated figures agree with one another and with the published percentage increases.

SCOPE NOTES FOR USE
- 'From April 2026' is read as the rate taking effect on 1 April 2026 (the standard annual uprating date), not a rate announced in April 2026. In practice the figures were announced earlier — LPC advice 27 October 2025, accepted at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025 — so both readings converge on the same numbers.
- 'National Living Wage' here means the statutory NLW set under the National Minimum Wage Act 1998. It is not the Living Wage Foundation's voluntary 'Real Living Wage', which ONS records as £13.45 per hour outside London and £14.80 per hour in London in April 2026. Do not substitute those figures.
- Age bands in force for 2026/27: NLW for 21 and over; 18-20 Year Old Rate for 18, 19 and 20 year olds; 16-17 Year Old Rate for those above school leaving age but under 18; Apprentice Rate for apprentices under 19, or 19 and over in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year is entitled to the NLW (£12.71), not the apprentice rate.
- The rate that governs compliance is the one in force on the date the work is performed, not the date pay is processed. Work performed on or before 31 March 2026 is governed by the 2025/26 rates (NLW £12.21; 18-20 £10.00; under 18 £7.55; apprentice £7.55; accommodation offset £10.66). Work performed on or after 1 April 2026 is governed by the rates above. Any pay period straddling 1 April 2026 must be apportioned.
- The 18-20 Year Old Rate remains in force for 2026/27. The LPC has noted the Government's stated policy of eventually removing that band, but that has no effect on the £10.85 rate applicable from 1 April 2026.
- April 2027 rates (£13.21 for 21 and over; £11.27 for 18-20) are already published and are shown here only to distinguish them from the requested 2026 figures.

Drivers using a sleeper berth must take at least 8 hours in the sleeper berth, and may split the sleeper berth time into two periods provided neither is less than 2 hours. All sleeper berth pairings MUST add up to at least 8 hours.

Drivers are allowed to extend the 11-hour maximum driving limit and 14-hour driving window by up to 2 hours when adverse driving conditions are encountered.

On June 1, 2020, FMCSA revised four provisions of the hours of service regulations to provide greater flexibility for drivers without adversely affecting safety. Motor carriers are required to comply with the new HOS regulations starting on September 29, 2020.
